subject: Science
chapter: The Living World : Adaptations and Classification
notes: Plants and animals show great diversity in shape, size, colour and habitat.
Adaptation is a gradual change in body parts or behaviour that helps an organism survive in its environment.
Desert plants have thick stems, small or needle‑like leaves, waxy coating and deep roots to conserve water.
Aquatic plants have floating leaves, hollow stems, waxy surfaces and air spaces for buoyancy.
Snowy‑region plants are conical with sloping branches to shed snow and have thick bark for cold protection.
Forest plants grow tall or climb to reach light; climbers use tendrils and vines for support.
Grassland plants have fibrous roots that prevent soil erosion and provide food for herbivores.
Parasitic plants like dodder lack chlorophyll and obtain nutrients from host plants via haustorial roots.
Carnivorous plants (e.g., Venus flytrap) attract insects with sticky surfaces and trap them for nitrogen.
Animals adapt by developing specialised body parts: fins for fish, webbed feet for ducks, claws for predators, and camouflage for prey.
Fish have gills, scales, streamlined bodies and air bladders for buoyancy.
Frogs have webbed toes, permeable skin for breathing underwater and bright colours for camouflage.
Herbivores have flat teeth and wide‑angle vision; carnivores have sharp teeth and forward‑placed eyes for depth perception.
Desert animals have thick skin, long legs, folded nostrils and nocturnal habits to avoid heat.
Snowy‑region animals have white or thick fur for insulation and camouflage.
Birds have hollow bones, feathers, a light body and wings for flight; bats use a patagium between limbs.
Reptiles have scaly skin and use muscles for creeping; snakes have no limbs and rely on body undulation.
Adaptations are inherited traits that increase survival and are passed to the next generation (Darwin’s natural selection).
Classification groups living things into Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
Binomial nomenclature gives each species a two‑part scientific name: genus + species.
The hierarchy of classification is based on shared characteristics and evolutionary relationships.
Understanding adaptations helps explain why organisms are suited to their habitats.

quiz.q: Which plant adaptation helps it survive in desert conditions?
quiz.explain: Desert plants have thick, fleshy stems that store water.

quiz.q: What feature helps fish stay buoyant in water?
quiz.explain: An air bladder allows fish to control buoyancy.

quiz.explain: The waxy layer reduces evaporation of water.

quiz.explain: Camels can travel long distances in deserts carrying loads.

quiz.q: Which part of a plant is responsible for absorbing water and nutrients?
quiz.explain: Roots absorb water and nutrients from soil.

quiz.q: What adaptation allows birds to fly efficiently?
quiz.explain: Feathers provide lift; hollow bones reduce weight.

quiz.q: Which of these is a feature of amphibians?
quiz.explain: Amphibians have webbed toes for swimming.

quiz.q: What does binomial nomenclature consist of?
quiz.explain: Scientific names have two parts: genus + species.

subject: Science
notes: Disasters are events that cause loss of life or property.
There are two main types: natural (floods, earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunamis, storms, lightning, cloudbursts, famine) and man‑made (war, industrial accidents, pollution).
Natural disasters happen because of changes in weather or Earth’s interior; man‑made disasters result from human actions.
Famine is a severe shortage of food and water, often caused by drought but can be worsened by poor planning and overpopulation.
Water scarcity can be reduced by water‑saving practices, tree planting, and proper water management.
A cloudburst is a sudden, heavy rainfall (≥100 mm/h) over a small area, caused by rapid condensation of vapour.
Lightning is a discharge of static electricity between clouds or between a cloud and the ground; 95 % strike the ground.
Lightning can be dangerous because it heats air to 30 000 °C, causing a shock wave and fire.
Volcanoes erupt when hot magma, gas and ash escape the Earth’s crust; they can create new land and pollute the air.
Tsunami is a series of large waves generated by an underwater earthquake or volcanic eruption; they travel fast (800–900 km/h).
Floods occur when water overflows its banks; protective measures include dams, percolation tanks and river‑bed flattening.
Storms are intense weather systems with strong winds; safety measures include staying indoors and avoiding open ground.
Safety tips for lightning: stay indoors, avoid trees, poles, wires, and water; keep 15 ft distance between people.
Lightning conductors on buildings help direct the strike safely.
Earthquakes can trigger tsunamis if they occur under the sea; the energy pushes water upward.
Disaster management involves prediction, preparedness, response and recovery.
Community awareness and proper planning can reduce the impact of disasters.
The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) provides guidelines and information online.
UNDP and other international bodies support disaster‑risk reduction globally.
Remember: ‘No disaster is inevitable, but its impact can be minimized by knowledge and action.’

quiz.explain: Industrial accidents are man‑made disasters.

quiz.explain: About 95% of lightning strikes the ground.

quiz.explain: Small dams control flood water.

quiz.explain: Famine is mainly due to drought but can be worsened by other factors.

quiz.explain: It is a wave generated by an underwater seismic event.

subject: Science
notes: Cell is the smallest unit of life and the basic building block of all living organisms.
All living things are made up of cells – unicellular or multicellular.
The main parts of a cell are the cell wall (only in plant cells), cell membrane, cytoplasm and organelles.
Organelles are specialised structures inside a cell: nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, lysosomes, vacuoles, chloroplasts (in plants) and ribosomes.
The nucleus contains DNA and controls cell functions; it has a double membrane with pores.
Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell – they produce energy (ATP).
Chloroplasts in plant cells carry out photosynthesis, converting light energy into chemical energy.
Vacuoles store water, nutrients and waste; plant cells usually have one large central vacuole.
The cell membrane is a flexible, thin covering that controls what enters and leaves the cell.
Prokaryotic cells (bacteria, viruses) lack membrane‑bound organelles; they have a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and nucleoid.
Eukaryotic cells (plant and animal) have many organelles and a nucleus.
Micro‑organisms are tiny living organisms that can only be seen with a microscope; they include bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses.
Micro‑organisms are everywhere – in air, water, soil, food and even inside plants and animals.
Some micro‑organisms are useful (fermentation, antibiotics, waste decomposition) and some are harmful (food poisoning, diseases).
The human body temperature is about 37 °C, which is close to the optimum temperature (15–35 °C) for many micro‑organisms.
Micro‑organisms can survive in extreme conditions by forming a protective covering (spores).
Vaccines are made from harmless micro‑organisms or their parts and give immunity against specific diseases.
Antibiotics are medicines produced by micro‑organisms that kill or stop the growth of harmful bacteria.
Proper hygiene, food safety and waste disposal help prevent the spread of harmful micro‑organisms.

quiz.explain: The cell wall is a rigid outer layer found only in plant cells.

quiz.explain: Mitochondria generate ATP, the energy currency of the cell.

quiz.explain: The nucleoid is found only in prokaryotic cells.

quiz.explain: All listed micro‑organisms are too small to be seen without a microscope.

quiz.explain: Yeast is beneficial for fermentation in bread.

quiz.explain: The cell membrane regulates transport in and out of the cell.

quiz.explain: Lactic acid bacteria ferment lactose into yoghurt.

quiz.q: What does a vaccine do?
quiz.explain: Vaccines expose the immune system to harmless parts of a micro‑organism to build immunity.

quiz.explain: Bacterial cells are prokaryotic.

options: Wet waste is easier to compost
quiz.explain: Wet waste attracts pests and accelerates decomposition.

subject: Science
chapter: The Muscular System and Digestive System in Human Beings
notes: Muscles are bundles of fibres that contract and relax to move the body.
Skeletal muscles attach to bones via tendons and are under voluntary control.
Cardiac (heart) muscles contract rhythmically and are involuntary.
Smooth muscles line internal organs like stomach, intestines, blood vessels and work slowly and involuntarily.
The muscular system works in pairs: when one muscle contracts, its antagonist relaxes.
The largest muscle in the human body is the quadriceps femoris in the thigh.
The smallest muscle is the stapedius in the ear, which helps control sound vibration.
The digestive system converts food into nutrients that can be absorbed into the blood.
Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in digestion (e.g., amylase, pepsin).
The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid and pepsin to break down proteins.
Bile from the liver emulsifies fats in the small intestine.
The small intestine is about 6 m long and absorbs most nutrients.
The large intestine is about 1.5 m long and absorbs water and electrolytes.
The appendix is a small pouch attached to the large intestine and has no known digestive function.
Healthy habits like avoiding tobacco and alcohol keep the digestive system working well.

quiz.q: Which type of muscle is found in the heart?
quiz.explain: Heart muscle is cardiac and works involuntarily.

quiz.q: What is the main function of bile?
quiz.explain: Bile emulsifies fats for easier digestion.

quiz.q: Which organ secretes hydrochloric acid?
quiz.explain: The stomach’s gastric glands produce HCl.

quiz.q: Which muscle group helps lift the arm?
quiz.explain: Biceps contract to lift the arm at the elbow.

quiz.explain: The alimentary canal carries food through the digestive organs.

quiz.explain: Amylase (ptyalin) starts starch digestion in saliva.

quiz.explain: Skeletal muscles are controlled by will.

quiz.explain: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.

quiz.explain: The gall bladder stores bile until needed.

options: It is found only in the heart
It is the largest muscle in the body
quiz.explain: Smooth muscle moves slowly and is involuntary.

subject: Science
notes: - A *change* is a transformation of a material into a different state or substance.
- **Natural change** happens by itself (e.g., ripening of fruit, rusting of iron).
- **Man‑made change** is caused by human action (e.g., cooking, painting).
- **Useful change** benefits us (e.g., sharpening a pencil).
- **Harmful change** is damaging or useless (e.g., corrosion of metal).
- **Fast (quick) change** occurs in a short time (bursting of a balloon).
- **Slow change** takes a long time (ripening of fruit).
- **Reversible change** can go back and forth (melting and solidifying wax).
- **Irreversible change** cannot be undone (ripening of mango).
- **Periodic change** repeats at regular intervals (day‑night cycle).
- **Non‑periodic change** repeats irregularly or not at all (earthquake).
- **Physical change** keeps the same substance (melting ice, boiling water).
- **Chemical change** creates a new substance (rusting iron, burning wood).
- **Corrosion** is a chemical change that weakens metals (rust, green patina).
- **Evaporation** is a physical change where liquid turns to vapor (water in a bowl).
- **Dissolving, boiling, melting** are all physical changes.
- **Burning wood** is a chemical change that produces new substances (CO₂, ash).
- **Reversible changes** can be repeated (melting wax, dissolving sugar).
- **Irreversible changes** cannot be repeated (burning wood, rusting iron).
- **Physical changes** do not alter the chemical composition of the material.
- **Chemical changes** alter the chemical composition and produce new properties.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a natural change?
quiz.explain: Ripening of fruit occurs naturally without human intervention.

quiz.q: A balloon bursts in a few seconds. This is an example of a ___ change.
quiz.explain: Bursting happens quickly, so it is a fast change.

quiz.q: When iron rusts, it forms a reddish‑brown layer. This is an example of a ___ change.
quiz.explain: Rusting creates a new substance, so it is chemical.

quiz.q: Melting and then solidifying wax can be repeated many times. This is an example of a ___ change.
quiz.explain: The process can go back and forth, so it is reversible.

quiz.q: Which change is periodic?
quiz.explain: Day‑night cycle repeats at regular intervals.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a man‑made useful change?
quiz.explain: Cooking food is done by humans and is useful.

quiz.q: Which process is part of the water cycle?
quiz.explain: Evaporation is a key step in the water cycle.

quiz.q: Which change is irreversible?
quiz.explain: Burning wood produces new substances that cannot be undone.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a physical change?
quiz.explain: Melting ice changes state but not substance.

quiz.q: Which change is harmful?
quiz.explain: Burning wood can damage the material and is harmful.

subject: Science
notes: - Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
- All matter is made of tiny particles called atoms and molecules.
- States of matter: solid, liquid, gas.
- Change of state happens when temperature or pressure changes.
- Properties of matter: mass, volume, colour, smell, taste, texture, density, hardness, melting point, boiling point, conductivity, solubility, etc.
- Substance = matter made of one kind of atom or molecule.
- Mixture = matter made of two or more substances that can be separated by physical means.
- Element = substance whose molecules are made of only one type of atom (e.g., O, H, Fe).
- Compound = substance formed by chemical combination of two or more elements (e.g., H₂O, CO₂).
- Symbols of elements are one or two letters (H, O, Fe, Au).
- Metals are good conductors, malleable, ductile; non‑metals are poor conductors, brittle; metalloids have intermediate properties.
- Common separation methods: filtration, straining, sorting, winnowing, magnet, distillation, separating funnel, centrifugation, chromatography.
- Distillation separates liquids with different boiling points.
- Chromatography separates components based on solubility and adhesion to paper.
- A compound has a fixed composition; a mixture does not.
- The smallest particle of a compound is a molecule.
- Elements cannot be created or destroyed (law of conservation of mass).
- The symbol of an element is the first letter of its name, sometimes two letters if needed (Cl for chlorine).
- Water is a compound (H₂O) and can be a solvent for many mixtures.
- The mass of a substance is measured with a balance; volume is measured with a graduated cylinder or by displacement.
- The density of a substance is its mass per unit volume; it helps identify substances.
- The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which it turns into vapour.
- The melting point of a solid is the temperature at which it turns into liquid.
- The colour of a substance is a property of its molecules.
- The taste and smell of food are properties of the molecules present.

quiz.q: What is the smallest particle of a compound?
quiz.explain: A molecule is the smallest particle of a compound.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a mixture?
quiz.explain: Air is a mixture of gases.

quiz.q: Which property can be measured with a balance?
quiz.explain: Mass is measured with a balance.

quiz.q: Which of these is an element?
quiz.explain: Oxygen gas is an element.

quiz.q: What does the symbol 'Fe' stand for?
quiz.explain: Fe is the symbol for iron.

quiz.q: Which method separates liquids with different boiling points?
quiz.explain: Distillation separates liquids by boiling point.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a compound and a mixture?
options: Compounds are pure, mixtures are impure
Compounds are made of one element, mixtures of many
Compounds have fixed composition, mixtures do not
Mixtures are always liquids, compounds are solids
quiz.explain: Compounds have a fixed composition; mixtures do not.

quiz.q: Which of these is a metalloid?
quiz.explain: Silicon is a metalloid.

quiz.q: What property of a substance is used in chromatography?
quiz.explain: Chromatography uses solubility and adhesion.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a separation method?
quiz.explain: Combining is not a separation method.

subject: Science
notes: Natural materials are those found in nature, like wood, stone, and metal.
Man‑made materials are produced by humans, e.g. plastics, synthetic detergents, and cement.
Toothpaste contains calcium carbonate, calcium hydrogen phosphate, and fluoride; fluoride prevents tooth decay.
Detergents are surface‑active substances that can mix oil and water; they form a milky mixture when added to oil‑water mix.
Soap is a natural detergent made from fats and alkali; it is a sodium or potassium salt of fatty acids.
Hard water contains calcium and magnesium ions; soap forms scum in hard water and does not lather well.
Synthetic detergents are made from fats or kerosene and work well even in hard water.
Cement is a dry, greenish‑grey powder made from lime, silica, alumina, iron oxide and gypsum; Portland cement is the most common type.
Concrete is made by mixing cement, water, sand and gravel; it is used for roads and buildings because it is strong and durable.
Surface activity is the ability of a substance to spread on a surface; it is responsible for lather formation in soaps and detergents.
Key ingredients of toothpaste: abrasives (calcium carbonate) to clean, fluoride to strengthen enamel, and humectants to keep it moist.
Key ingredients of cement: lime (calcium oxide), silica (silicon dioxide), alumina, iron oxide and gypsum.
Natural detergents (soap nut, soap pod) contain saponin and are gentle on skin.
Hard soap is a sodium salt of fatty acids; soft soap is a potassium salt of fatty acids.
The first commercial toothpaste was made by Colgate in 1873.
Synthetic detergents can be used in both soft and hard water.
Cement production involves heating limestone to 1400°C to make clinker, then grinding with gypsum.
Concrete’s hardness comes from the chemical reaction of cement with water (hydration).

quiz.q: Which ingredient in toothpaste helps prevent tooth decay?
quiz.explain: Fluoride strengthens enamel and prevents decay.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a detergent?
options: To clean or wipe away dirt
quiz.explain: Detergents remove dirt by mixing oil and water.

quiz.q: Which type of soap is used for bathing?
quiz.explain: Soft soap is a potassium salt of fatty acids, gentle for bathing.

quiz.q: What is the main component of Portland cement?
quiz.explain: Portland cement contains about 60% lime (calcium oxide).

quiz.q: Why does soap not lather well in hard water?
options: It reacts with calcium and magnesium ions
quiz.explain: Calcium and magnesium ions form insoluble scum with soap.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a natural detergent?
quiz.explain: Soap nut contains saponin and is a natural detergent.

quiz.q: What is surface activity?
options: The ability to spread on a surface
The ability to dissolve in water
quiz.explain: Surface activity allows a substance to spread and form lather.

quiz.q: Which material is NOT used in concrete?
quiz.explain: Concrete is made from cement, water, sand and gravel, not paper.

quiz.q: What is the main role of fluoride in toothpaste?
quiz.explain: Fluoride strengthens enamel and prevents cavities.

quiz.q: Which type of soap is a sodium salt of fatty acids?
quiz.explain: Hard soap is a sodium salt of fatty acids.

subject: Science
notes: Natural resources are substances obtained from nature that satisfy human needs, such as soil, stones, minerals, air, water, plants and animals.
The Earth’s lithosphere is the outer solid shell made of land and the upper part of the crust where minerals and ores are found.
Minerals are solid crystals with a definite chemical composition and crystal structure; ores are minerals that contain a valuable metal in sufficient quantity to be mined economically.
Minerals are classified as non‑metallic (e.g., quartz, mica) and metallic (e.g., iron, copper).
Minerals can be formed by crystallisation from magma, by precipitation from water, or by transformation of organic matter (e.g., coal, oil, gas).
Coal is a fossil fuel formed from buried plant material under pressure and heat over millions of years.
Mineral oil (petroleum) and natural gas are formed from the decomposition of ancient marine organisms under high pressure and temperature.
Fossil fuels are non‑renewable energy sources that release carbon dioxide when burnt, contributing to climate change.
Forests are large areas covered by trees and plants; they provide timber, food, medicine, and protect soil and water resources.
Marine resources include dissolved minerals (e.g., sodium, potassium), marine life (fish, shellfish), and hydrocarbons (oil, gas) found in seawater and seabed.
Energy can be harnessed from oceans by tidal power, wave power and ocean currents.
Conservation of forests involves protecting young trees, planting more trees than are cut, and enforcing strict regulations.
Medicinal plants such as neem, tulsi, and cinnamon have therapeutic uses like treating cough, fever and cancer.
The economic condition of a nation depends on its natural resources because they provide raw materials, energy, and employment opportunities.
Alternative fuels such as hydrogen, biofuels and methanol are being explored as fossil fuels become scarce.

quiz.q: What is a natural resource?
options: A substance that can be used for energy
A material that is found only in factories
quiz.explain: Natural resources are substances obtained from nature.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a natural resource?
quiz.explain: Plastic is a man‑made product, not a natural resource.

quiz.q: The earth’s outer layer that contains minerals is called the
quiz.explain: Lithosphere is the crust where minerals are found.

quiz.q: Which metal is found in the free state in nature?
quiz.explain: Gold occurs in a free state; most metals are in compounds.

quiz.q: What term describes minerals that contain a high proportion of metal?
quiz.explain: Ores are mineral deposits rich in metal.

quiz.q: Which of these is a fossil fuel?
quiz.explain: Natural gas is a fossil fuel formed from ancient organisms.

quiz.q: Which ocean resource is used for producing soap and glass?
quiz.explain: Potassium is used in soap and glass production.

quiz.q: Which type of coal is of the highest grade?
quiz.explain: Anthracite is the highest grade of coal.

quiz.q: Why is mineral oil called a liquid fuel?
options: It is liquid at room temperature
It is made of liquid water
quiz.explain: Mineral oil is liquid at normal temperatures.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an eco‑friendly fuel?
quiz.explain: Natural gas emits less CO₂ and is considered eco‑friendly.

subject: Science
notes: Light is a form of energy that travels in waves.
A beam of light can be seen when it is scattered by particles in the air or in a liquid.
Scattering of light is the redirection of light rays by tiny particles or molecules.
Blue light is scattered more than red light because its wavelength is shorter.
The sky appears blue during the day because blue sunlight is scattered in all directions.
At sunrise and sunset the light passes through a longer path in the atmosphere, so more blue light is scattered and the sky looks red or orange.
A shadow is the dark area produced when an opaque object blocks light.
The dark part of a shadow is called the umbra.
The lighter part of a shadow, where only part of the light is blocked, is called the penumbra.
A point light source produces a sharp, well‑defined shadow with a clear umbra.
An extended light source produces a softer shadow with both a penumbra and an umbra.
During a solar eclipse the moon passes between the sun and the earth, casting the moon’s shadow on the earth.
During a lunar eclipse the earth passes between the sun and the moon, casting the earth’s shadow on the moon.
The zero‑shadow day occurs when the sun is directly overhead and shadows disappear at noon.
Eclipses can be total, partial or annular depending on how the shadows overlap.
Observing a solar eclipse with the naked eye can damage the eyes; special glasses are required.
The colour of a laser beam is visible only when it is scattered by particles.
The colour of the sky is a result of the scattering of sunlight by air molecules and dust.
The blue colour of the sky is due to Rayleigh scattering.
The red colour of the sunset is due to the scattering of blue light and the direct transmission of red light.

quiz.q: Which colour of sunlight is scattered the most by the atmosphere?
quiz.explain: Blue light has a shorter wavelength and is scattered more strongly (Rayleigh scattering).

quiz.q: What is the dark part of a shadow called?
quiz.explain: The umbra is the region where all light from the source is blocked.

quiz.q: During a solar eclipse, why can we not look directly at the sun?
quiz.explain: The sun’s rays are intense and can harm the retina.

quiz.q: What happens to the colour of the sky at sunset?
quiz.explain: Blue light is scattered out of the line of sight, leaving red and orange hues.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of eclipse?
quiz.explain: Mercury eclipse is not a real astronomical event.

quiz.q: What is the term for the part of a shadow where only part of the light is blocked?
quiz.explain: The penumbra is the lighter fringe of a shadow.

quiz.q: Why is a laser beam visible in turbid water but not in clear water?
options: The beam is scattered by particles
The beam is absorbed by the beaker
quiz.explain: Scattering by particles makes the beam visible.

quiz.q: What is the name of the event when the moon passes between the sun and the earth?
quiz.explain: A solar eclipse occurs when the moon blocks the sun.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes a point light source?
quiz.explain: A point source gives a well‑defined umbra.

quiz.q: What is the zero‑shadow day?
options: When the sun is at the horizon
When the sun is directly overhead
quiz.explain: At noon the sun is overhead and shadows vanish.

subject: Science
notes: Sound is produced when an object vibrates and the vibration moves the surrounding medium (air, water, solids).
The vibration causes the particles of the medium to oscillate, creating a wave that travels to our ears.
A sound wave is a longitudinal wave: particles of the medium move back and forth in the same direction as the wave travels.
The frequency of vibration (cycles per second) determines the pitch of the sound: higher frequency = higher pitch.
The amplitude of vibration determines the intensity (loudness) of the sound: larger amplitude = louder sound.
The time taken for one complete vibration is called the period (T). Frequency (f) is the number of vibrations per second: f = 1/T.
The unit of frequency is Hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = one vibration per second.
Sound needs a medium; in vacuum there is no sound because there are no particles to vibrate.
The audible range for humans is about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Below 20 Hz is infrasonic, above 20 000 Hz is ultrasonic.
The decibel (dB) is a logarithmic unit for sound level. A 10 dB increase means the intensity is ten times greater.
When the amplitude of a vibration is doubled, the intensity increases by a factor of four (10 dB).
Tuning an instrument changes the tension of its strings or diaphragm, which changes the frequency of vibration.
A pendulum’s period increases as its length increases; its frequency decreases with length.
The sound produced by a string is higher when the tension is increased and lower when the tension is decreased.
The vibration of a rubber band or a pendulum is an example of an oscillator and oscillatory motion.
The sound produced by a vibrating object is heard when the vibration causes the surrounding medium to oscillate in the audible frequency range.
In a musical instrument, the part that vibrates (strings, air column, membrane) is the sound source.
The intensity of sound is proportional to the square of the amplitude of vibration.
The pitch of a sound is directly related to its frequency.
Infrasonic sounds (below 20 Hz) are used by animals like elephants for long‑range communication.
Ultrasonic sounds (above 20 000 Hz) can be heard by some animals like dogs and bats.
The human ear cannot detect sound in a vacuum because there is no medium to transmit vibrations.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes how a musical instrument produces sound?
quiz.explain: Sound is produced when an object vibrates, creating pressure waves in the air.

quiz.q: What is the unit of frequency?
quiz.explain: Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz), the number of oscillations per second.

quiz.q: If the amplitude of a vibrating string is doubled, how does the intensity of the sound change?
quiz.explain: Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so doubling amplitude makes intensity four times.

quiz.q: Which sound has a higher pitch: a lion’s roar or a mosquito’s hum?
quiz.explain: Higher pitch corresponds to higher frequency; a lion’s roar is much higher in frequency than a mosquito’s hum.

quiz.q: What happens to the pitch of a string when its tension is increased?
quiz.explain: Increasing tension raises the frequency, producing a higher pitch.

quiz.q: A sound with a frequency of 25 Hz is considered:
quiz.explain: Frequencies below 20 Hz are infrasonic; 25 Hz is just above that but still below audible range.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a factor that affects the intensity of sound?
quiz.explain: Intensity depends on amplitude, distance, and medium, not on color.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between the length of a pendulum and its frequency?
options: Frequency is maximum at medium length
quiz.explain: A longer pendulum has a lower frequency (longer period).

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of ultrasonic sound?
quiz.explain: Bats emit ultrasonic frequencies above 20,000 Hz for echolocation.

quiz.q: The decibel scale is:
quiz.explain: Decibel values are logarithmic, representing ratios of intensities.

subject: Science
notes: - A magnet has two ends called the north pole and the south pole.
- Like poles (north–north or south–south) repel each other.
- Opposite poles (north–south) attract each other.
- Magnets are made from alloys of iron, cobalt and nickel. Examples are Nipermag (iron, nickel, aluminium, titanium) and Alnico (aluminium, nickel, cobalt).
- A freely suspended magnet always points north‑south because the Earth is a giant magnet with its magnetic north near the geographic south pole.
- The Earth’s magnetic field is the region around it where magnetic forces act on a magnet or a magnetic needle.
- Magnetic field lines are imaginary lines that start at the north pole and end at the south pole of a magnet.
- Magnetic field lines never cross each other and are dense where the field is strong.
- A magnet can attract objects at a distance; this is called magnetic force.
- Magnetic force is a vector quantity (has magnitude and direction).
- A magnetic field can pass through non‑magnetic materials like cardboard, water and plastic, but its intensity decreases with distance.
- An electromagnet is a magnet made by passing electric current through a coil of wire around a ferromagnetic core.
- Electromagnets are used in metal detectors, cranes, and many industrial machines.
- The real test of a magnet is to see if it can repel another magnet or attract a compass needle.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a magnetic pole of a bar magnet?
quiz.explain: Bar magnets have only north and south poles.

quiz.q: What is the main reason a freely suspended magnet points north‑south?
options: It is attracted to the Earth’s magnetic field
It is attracted to the Earth’s gravity
It is attracted to the Sun
It is attracted to the Moon
quiz.explain: The Earth’s magnetic field aligns the magnet.

quiz.q: Which alloy is NOT used to make permanent magnets?
quiz.explain: Titanium alone is not a magnetic alloy.

quiz.q: Magnetic field lines run from which pole to which pole?
quiz.explain: Lines go from north to south.

quiz.q: What type of quantity is magnetic force?
quiz.explain: It has magnitude and direction.

quiz.q: Which material can a magnetic field pass through?
quiz.explain: Magnetic fields can penetrate non‑magnetic materials.

quiz.q: An electromagnet is made by:
quiz.explain: Electric current in a coil magnetises the core.

quiz.q: The real test of a magnet is to:
options: See if it attracts iron filings
See if it repels another magnet
See if it can be magnetised
quiz.explain: Repulsion shows like poles.

quiz.q: Which of these is a property of magnetic field lines?
options: They are dense where field is weak
They start at the south pole
quiz.explain: Lines repel like poles.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a magnet?
options: It has north and south poles
It can be made of aluminium
quiz.explain: Aluminium alone is not magnetic.

subject: Science
notes: Roots are the part of a plant that grows below the soil and absorb water and minerals.
The main types of roots are tap roots (single thick root) and fibrous roots (many thin roots).
Tap roots grow straight down and are common in dicotyledonous plants like peas and beans.
Fibrous roots spread out horizontally and are common in monocotyledonous plants like grasses and corn.
Roots have root hairs near the tips that increase surface area for absorption.
The root tip is protected by a root cap, a thin, cap‑like structure.
Adventitious roots grow from stems or leaves and can be aerial or breathing roots.
The stem is the main support of a plant and bears leaves, flowers and fruits.
Nodes are points on the stem where leaves or branches emerge; internodes are the segments between nodes.
Leaves are produced from nodes and have a blade (lamina) and a petiole (stalk).
Leaf margins can be entire, dentate (toothed) or lobed.
Simple leaves have one undivided blade; compound leaves have several leaflets.
Leaf venation can be parallel (as in maize) or reticulate (as in peepal).
Flowers have a calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (male part) and gynoecium (female part).
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma, leading to fertilisation.
Fruits develop from the ovary after fertilisation and contain seeds.
Seeds can be dicotyledonous (two seed leaves) or monocotyledonous (one seed leaf).
Plants use roots for anchorage, absorption, storage and sometimes for special functions like breathing or support.

quiz.q: Which part of a seed grows into the root?
quiz.explain: The radicle is the embryonic root that emerges first.

quiz.q: What type of root do monocotyledonous plants usually have?
quiz.explain: Monocots like maize have fibrous root systems.

quiz.q: Which structure protects the root tip?
quiz.explain: The root cap shields the delicate root tip.

quiz.q: What is the main function of leaf veins?
quiz.explain: Veins carry water, nutrients and sugars.

quiz.q: Which leaf type has a single undivided blade?
quiz.explain: A simple leaf has one blade.

quiz.q: In a flower, the male reproductive part is called the
quiz.explain: Androecium contains stamens.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a part of the calyx?
quiz.explain: Petals belong to the corolla.

quiz.q: Which leaf venation pattern is seen in maize?
quiz.explain: Maize leaves have parallel veins.

quiz.q: What happens when the root tip is injured?
quiz.explain: Damage to the root tip stops its growth.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a spiny stem?
quiz.explain: Cacti have spiny stems for protection.

subject: Science
notes: A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity.
The Milky Way is our galaxy; it contains hundreds of billions of stars.
Stars form from nebulae – clouds of hydrogen and dust that collapse under gravity.
When a cloud contracts, its core temperature rises until nuclear fusion starts, creating a new star.
The life of a star is called its lifecycle; it changes slowly over millions of years.
Low‑mass stars become red dwarfs and later white dwarfs after shedding outer layers as planetary nebulae.
High‑mass stars explode as supernovae and may leave behind neutron stars or black holes.
The Sun is a medium‑size star in the middle of its lifecycle, about 4.6 billion years old.
Constellations are patterns of stars that appear close together from Earth’s point of view.
The celestial sphere is an imaginary sphere around Earth on which all stars are projected.
The horizon is the line where the sky meets the ground; it forms a circle when seen from a point on Earth.
The zenith is the point on the celestial sphere directly above you; the nadir is directly below.
Celestial poles are points where Earth’s rotation axis meets the celestial sphere; they are north and south poles of the sky.
The meridian is a great circle passing through the celestial poles, your zenith and nadir.
The celestial equator is the projection of Earth’s equator onto the celestial sphere; it divides the sky into northern and southern halves.
The ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun on the celestial sphere, 23.5° tilted to the celestial equator.
The Sun appears to move east to west because Earth rotates west to east.
The Pole Star (Polaris) is almost fixed in the sky and is used to find north in the northern hemisphere.
Zodiac signs are 12 equal parts of the ecliptic, each 30° wide, named after constellations like Aries, Taurus, etc.
Nakshatras are 27 lunar mansions in Indian astronomy; each covers about 13°20' of the ecliptic.
The brightest star in a constellation is often called its main star or reference point.
The Sun’s apparent motion is called its apparent path; it is due to Earth’s orbit around the Sun.
Observing the sky requires a clear view, a dark environment, and knowledge of constellations and celestial coordinates.
Sky watching helps students learn about the motion of Earth and the Sun and the structure of the galaxy.

quiz.q: What is the main component of a nebula that forms stars?
quiz.explain: Nebulae are mainly composed of hydrogen gas and dust particles.

quiz.q: Which star is used as a reference point for finding north in the northern hemisphere?
quiz.explain: Polaris, the Pole Star, is almost fixed in the sky and indicates north.

quiz.q: The path the Sun appears to follow on the celestial sphere is called the:
quiz.explain: The ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun.

quiz.q: A white dwarf is the remnant of which type of star?
quiz.explain: Low‑mass stars become white dwarfs after shedding outer layers.

quiz.q: How many zodiac signs are there on the ecliptic?
quiz.explain: The ecliptic is divided into 12 zodiac signs, each 30° wide.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of a galaxy?
quiz.explain: Planets are not a major component of a galaxy; they orbit stars.

quiz.q: The point on the celestial sphere directly below you is called the:
quiz.explain: Nadir is directly below you on the celestial sphere.

quiz.q: Which of these is a type of constellation used in Indian astronomy?
quiz.explain: Nakshatra refers to the 27 lunar mansions in Indian astronomy.

quiz.q: The Sun’s apparent motion is caused by the:
quiz.explain: The apparent motion is due to Earth’s orbit around the Sun.

quiz.q: Which star is the brightest in the constellation Orion?
quiz.explain: Betelgeuse is the bright red supergiant in Orion.

subject: Science
notes: Air is a mixture of gases (nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide) and tiny particles of dust and water vapour.
Air is a homogeneous mixture – its composition is the same everywhere in a small region.
The weight of air can be felt when a stick with balloons is tilted; the stick moves because air has mass.
Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted by air on a surface; it is about 1.01×10^5 N/m² at sea level.
Pressure decreases with height above sea level.
Bernoulli’s principle: when the speed of a fluid (air) increases, its pressure decreases, and vice versa.
A pressure difference makes air flow from high pressure to low pressure – this is wind or breeze.
When the temperature of air rises, its density falls and the pressure at a given height falls.
When the temperature of air falls, its density rises and the pressure at a given height rises.
Water vapour in air can condense into droplets when the air cools – this is dew.
Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats; this is because water expands when it freezes below 4 °C (anomalous behaviour).
Water expands by about 9 % when it freezes; its density at 4 °C is 1 g/cm³, the maximum density.
Water is a universal solvent – it can dissolve many substances because of its polarity.
Soil colour depends on organic matter and mineral content; it helps indicate soil fertility and drainage.
Sandy soil drains quickly but holds little nutrients; clay soil holds water but is hard to plough; silt soil is intermediate.
The pH of soil indicates acidity (pH<6.5), neutrality (6.5–7.5) or alkalinity (pH>7.5).
Good soil structure gives roots oxygen, good drainage and allows roots to grow well.
Sound needs a medium; in space there is no air, so sound cannot travel.
The density of seawater is higher than that of rainwater because salt increases its mass for the same volume.

quiz.q: Which gas is present in the highest proportion in air?
quiz.explain: Nitrogen makes up about 78 % of air.

quiz.q: What is the main reason air has weight?
options: It is a mixture of gases
quiz.explain: Air has mass because it is a mixture of gases.

quiz.q: When air flows from a high‑pressure region to a low‑pressure region, what phenomenon occurs?
quiz.explain: The flow of air from high to low pressure is wind.

quiz.q: According to Bernoulli’s principle, what happens to the pressure of a fluid when its speed increases?
quiz.explain: Higher speed means lower pressure.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a property of water?
quiz.explain: Water has no definite shape.

quiz.q: Why does ice float on water?
options: It is the same density as water
quiz.explain: Ice is less dense than liquid water.

quiz.q: What is the maximum density of water?
quiz.explain: At 4 °C water’s density is 1.0 g/cm³.

quiz.q: Which soil type has the highest water‑holding capacity?
quiz.explain: Clay soil holds the most water.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a reason for soil fertility loss?
quiz.explain: Saline water reduces fertility.

quiz.q: Sound cannot be heard in space because
quiz.explain: Sound needs a medium to travel.

subject: Science
notes: Nutrition is the process of taking in food and using it for energy, growth and repair.
Living organisms need nutrients to build tissues, produce energy and maintain health.
Nutrients are classified into macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) and micronutrients (minerals, vitamins).
Carbohydrates are the main energy source; proteins build and repair tissues; fats store energy and protect organs.
Minerals such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, iron, manganese, zinc are essential for plant growth.
Vitamins are organic compounds that act as co‑enzymes in many biochemical reactions.
Autotrophic nutrition: plants and some bacteria produce their own food through photosynthesis.
Heterotrophic nutrition: animals, fungi, many bacteria obtain food from other organisms.
Photosynthesis uses light energy, water, CO₂ and chlorophyll to produce glucose and oxygen: 6CO₂+6H₂O+light→C₆H₁₂O₆+6O₂.
Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N₂ into usable forms; done by root‑nodules (rhizobium) and free‑living bacteria (azotobacter).
Symbiotic nutrition: mutualistic relationships like lichens (fungus + algae) or mycorrhizae (fungus + plant roots).
Parasitic plants (e.g., cuscuta, loranthus) attach to host plants to obtain water and nutrients.
Insectivorous plants (e.g., Drosera) trap insects to supplement nitrogen in poor soils.
Saprophytic organisms (fungi, bacteria) decompose dead matter and recycle nutrients.
Animals ingest food by chewing, sucking, scraping, etc.; digestion breaks food into simple molecules for absorption.
Deficiency of nitrogen causes stunted growth and yellowing; phosphorus deficiency leads to poor root development; potassium deficiency weakens stems.
Plants show specific symptoms of mineral deficiency: yellowing of leaves, early leaf fall, weak stems, etc.

quiz.q: What is malnutrition?
options: A state of having too much food
A state of having insufficient or imbalanced food
quiz.explain: Malnutrition means not getting enough or the right balance of nutrients.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a macro‑nutrient?
quiz.explain: Vitamin C is a micro‑nutrient, not a macro‑nutrient.

quiz.q: What is autotrophic nutrition?
quiz.explain: Autotrophic nutrition is when an organism makes its own food, e.g., plants via photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Which gas is released as a by‑product of photosynthesis?
quiz.explain: Photosynthesis releases oxygen.

quiz.q: Which organ of a plant transports water from roots to leaves?
quiz.explain: Xylem carries water upward.

quiz.q: Which type of nitrogen fixation occurs in the soil by bacteria like Azotobacter?
quiz.explain: Azotobacter fixes nitrogen biologically in the soil.

quiz.q: Which plant is an example of a parasitic plant that is completely dependent on its host?
quiz.explain: Cuscuta (dodder) is a fully parasitic plant.

quiz.q: What is the main function of the phloem in plants?
quiz.explain: Phloem moves sugars from leaves to other parts.

quiz.q: Which animal type feeds on dead bodies of other animals?
quiz.explain: Scavengers eat dead animals.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of heterotrophic plants?
quiz.explain: Heterotrophic plants lack chlorophyll and rely on other organisms for food.

subject: Science
notes: Food contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water – all needed for growth.
Carbohydrates give energy; proteins build and repair tissues; fats store energy and protect organs.
Vitamins are organic compounds needed in small amounts; minerals are inorganic elements like iron and calcium.
Fibre helps digestion and keeps the gut healthy.
Water keeps body temperature normal and transports nutrients.
Food spoilage is a change in colour, odour, texture or taste caused by microbes, insects, chemicals or improper handling.
Spoiled food can make us sick – symptoms include nausea, vomiting and stomach pain.
Food preservation slows down or stops spoilage by using methods like freezing, drying, boiling, smoking, adding preservatives or irradiation.
Pasteurisation heats food (e.g., milk) to 72 °C for 15 s to kill harmful microbes while keeping taste.
Adulteration is adding harmful or useless substances (e.g., sand, iron filings) or removing useful parts (e.g., fat from milk).
To detect adulteration, simple tests include adding water to milk and looking for separation, using a magnet to find iron filings, or adding acid to see colour change.
Proper storage (cool, dry, sealed) and checking expiry dates help keep food safe.
Avoid over‑cooking and over‑serving; use leftovers wisely to reduce waste.
When buying food, buy only what you need and store it properly to prevent spoilage.
Food safety is important for everyone – young, old, rich or poor – because contaminated food can cause illness or death.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) sets rules for safe food handling and storage.
Freezing keeps food safe by stopping microbial growth; drying removes water that microbes need.
Smoking adds flavour and preserves food by depositing chemicals that inhibit microbes.
Irradiation uses high‑energy rays to kill microbes and insects in food.
Chemical preservatives like sodium benzoate, citric acid and vinegar keep food safe for a long time.
Natural preservatives include salt, sugar and oil, which reduce water activity and stop microbial growth.
Food safety education helps us make better choices and protect our health.
Food waste can be reduced by planning meals, using leftovers, and storing food correctly.
When food is stored at 5 °C, it stays safe for a short period; longer storage needs refrigeration or freezing.
A balanced diet with fresh fruits and vegetables reduces the risk of food‑borne diseases.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a nutrient found in food?
quiz.explain: Gravity is not a nutrient.

quiz.q: Food spoilage is mainly caused by which of the following?
quiz.explain: Micro‑organisms are the main cause of spoilage.

quiz.q: Which method of preservation involves lowering the temperature to slow down microbial growth?
quiz.explain: Freezing keeps food safe by reducing microbial activity.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of adding salt to food?
quiz.explain: Salt acts as a natural preservative.

quiz.q: Which of these is a chemical preservative used in jams?
quiz.explain: Sodium benzoate is a common chemical preservative.

quiz.q: What does pasteurisation primarily do?
quiz.explain: Pasteurisation kills microbes to extend shelf life.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of qualitative food wastage?
options: Serving too much food at a banquet
quiz.explain: Over‑cooking is a qualitative waste.

quiz.q: Which substance is used in the smoking method of food preservation?
quiz.explain: Aluminium phosphide is used for smoking.

quiz.q: What is the main effect of irradiation on food?
quiz.explain: Irradiation destroys microbes and insects.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a factor that causes food spoilage?
quiz.explain: Gravity does not cause spoilage.

subject: Science
notes: Mass is a scalar quantity – it has only magnitude, no direction.
Weight is a vector quantity – it has magnitude and direction (downward).
Weight depends on gravity; it changes with altitude and latitude.
Length, time, mass, temperature, volume, speed, density are physical quantities.
Units express the magnitude of a quantity: metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, Kelvin (K) for temperature, litre (L) for volume.
Standard units are fixed by international agreements (e.g., SI system).
The metre was originally defined by a platinum‑iridium bar; now by the speed of light.
The kilogram is defined by a platinum‑iridium prototype kept in Paris.
The second is defined by the frequency of a cesium‑133 atom (atomic clock).
The Kelvin is defined by the triple point of water.
The ampere is defined by the force between two conductors; the candela by luminous intensity.
Measurement accuracy depends on the purpose; use appropriate instruments.
Errors arise from using wrong devices, improper use, and lack of standardisation.
Standardisation ensures fair trade and scientific consistency.
In everyday life we use hand‑span, foot, yard, etc., but these are not reliable units.
The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) maintains standards worldwide.
The speed of light (≈3.0×10^8 m/s) is used to define the metre.
The concept of scalar vs. vector is important for understanding physical laws.
Weight varies on different planets because gravitational acceleration differs.
Mass remains constant anywhere because it is the amount of matter.
Standard units are crucial for accurate measurement in science and commerce.

quiz.q: Which quantity is a scalar?
quiz.explain: Mass has only magnitude, no direction.

quiz.q: Weight of an object is greatest at the poles because
options: Earth is flatter at the poles
Gravity is stronger at the poles
Atmosphere is denser at the poles
Temperature is lower at the poles
quiz.explain: Gravitational acceleration is slightly higher at the poles.

quiz.q: The metre was originally defined by
quiz.explain: A platinum‑iridium bar was the prototype.

quiz.q: Which unit is used to measure temperature in SI?
quiz.explain: Kelvin is the SI unit for temperature.

quiz.q: Speed is the ratio of
quiz.explain: Speed = distance ÷ time.

quiz.q: An atomic clock is kept in a
quiz.explain: Atomic clocks are kept in national labs.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
quiz.explain: Velocity has magnitude and direction.

quiz.q: The SI system is also known as the
quiz.explain: SI stands for International System of Units.

quiz.q: The unit of volume in SI is
quiz.explain: Litre is the SI unit for volume.

quiz.q: Which device measures mass accurately in shops?
quiz.explain: A digital or mechanical balance measures mass.

subject: Science
notes: Motion is a change in position of a body over time.
A force applied to a body causes a change in its motion.
Distance is the total length travelled, a scalar quantity measured in metres.
Displacement is the shortest straight‑line distance between start and end points, a vector quantity measured in metres.
Speed is the magnitude of motion, calculated as distance divided by time (m/s).
Velocity is speed with a direction, calculated as displacement divided by time (m/s).
Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time; instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a particular instant.
Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time (m/s²).
Force is a push or pull that can change the velocity of a body; it is a vector quantity measured in Newtons (N).
Work is done when a force causes a displacement; W = F × s (Joules).
If no external force acts, a body moves with constant velocity (Newton’s First Law).
The unit of work in SI is the Joule, where 1 J = 1 N × 1 m.
Work can be positive, negative or zero depending on the direction of force relative to displacement.
Energy is the capacity to do work; kinetic energy is associated with motion.
In a frictionless surface, a body will continue moving with constant velocity if no net force acts.
The magnitude of work depends on both the force applied and the distance over which it acts.
When a force is applied in the same direction as displacement, work is positive.
When a force is applied opposite to displacement, work is negative.
When a force is perpendicular to displacement, no work is done.

quiz.q: What is the unit of distance and displacement in the SI system?
quiz.explain: Distance and displacement are measured in metres.

quiz.q: Which quantity is a scalar?
quiz.explain: Distance is a scalar; displacement is a vector.

quiz.q: If a truck travels 40 km in 1 hour, what is its average velocity?
quiz.explain: Average velocity = total displacement / total time = 40 km / 1 h.

quiz.q: A body moves 1500 m in 25 minutes. What is its speed?
quiz.explain: Speed = distance / time = 1500 m / 1500 s = 1 m/s.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of acceleration?
quiz.explain: Mass does not cause acceleration; it resists changes in motion.

quiz.q: Work done by a force of 10 N moving a block 2 m in the direction of the force is
quiz.explain: Work = force × displacement = 10 N × 2 m = 20 J.

quiz.q: The unit of work in the CGS system is
quiz.explain: In CGS, work is measured in ergs.

quiz.q: A ball rolls from A to D in 4 seconds, covering 8 m. Its acceleration is
quiz.explain: Acceleration is zero because speed is constant (2 m/s).

quiz.q: Which statement is true about instantaneous velocity?
options: It is the same as average velocity.
It is the velocity at a specific instant.
quiz.explain: Instantaneous velocity refers to velocity at a particular moment.

quiz.q: According to Newton’s First Law, a body at rest will
options: Move if a force is applied.
Remain at rest if no net force acts.
Change direction if a force acts.
quiz.explain: Newton’s First Law states a body remains at rest or moves uniformly if no net force acts.

subject: Science
notes: Electric charge is a property of tiny particles inside all objects.
Each atom has a positive nucleus and negative electrons; normally they balance so the atom is neutral.
When two objects are rubbed, electrons move from one to the other, leaving one positively charged and the other negatively charged.
A positively charged object attracts negatively charged objects and repels other positive ones; the opposite holds for negative charges.
Like charges repel, unlike charges attract – this is called repulsion and attraction.
Static electricity is the build‑up of charge that stays on an object for a short time.
Frictional electricity is produced when two different materials rub against each other.
Induction is when a charged object causes a nearby neutral object to become charged without touching it.
A charged object can attract an uncharged object because the uncharged one becomes polarized.
A simple electroscope (copper rod with gold leaves) shows charge by the leaves opening apart.
Lightning is a huge discharge of static electricity between clouds and the ground.
A lightning conductor (copper rod with a pointed top) directs the charge safely into the earth.
The upper end of a lightning conductor is pointed to concentrate the electric field and attract the charge.
Coal and salt in the ground improve conductivity, spreading the charge into the earth.
When a charged comb is brought near flowing water, the water becomes temporarily charged and is attracted to the comb.
When a charged balloon touches an aluminium ball, both become charged in the same way (contact).
When a charged balloon is brought near an aluminium ball, the ball becomes oppositely charged by induction and they attract.
When a charged balloon touches an aluminium ball, the ball becomes similarly charged and they repel.
The earth is a huge reservoir of charge; a lightning strike transfers charge from the cloud to the earth.
Electrostatic experiments should be done in dry conditions because moisture dissipates the charge quickly.

quiz.q: What happens when a plastic comb is rubbed against a woollen cloth?
quiz.explain: Rubbing transfers electrons to the comb, giving it a negative charge.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a result of static electricity?
options: A spark between a charged blanket and a metal object
quiz.explain: Static electricity can cause a spark when a charged object touches a conductor.

quiz.q: Two objects with like charges do what when brought close?
quiz.explain: Like charges repel.

quiz.q: Which material is NOT likely to become charged by rubbing?
quiz.explain: Aluminium is a good conductor and tends to remain neutral when rubbed.

quiz.q: What is the main reason lightning is not seen everyday?
options: It requires a negatively charged cloud and a positively charged ground
It requires a positively charged cloud and a negatively charged ground
quiz.explain: Lightning occurs when a large charge difference exists between cloud and ground.

quiz.q: When a negatively charged comb is brought near flowing water, the water is attracted because
quiz.explain: Negative comb repels electrons in water, leaving a positive region that attracts the comb.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a correct statement about induction?
options: It transfers charge from one object to another
It creates a charge in an uncharged object by proximity
quiz.explain: Induction creates a charge in an uncharged object when a charged object is nearby.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the lightning conductor?
options: To conduct lightning into the ground
quiz.explain: It safely directs the current of lightning into the earth.

quiz.q: Which metal is commonly used for the leaves of an electroscope?
quiz.explain: Gold leaves are used because they are light and do not conduct away the charge quickly.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of static electricity?
options: It remains on an object for a short time
quiz.explain: Static electricity is produced by friction and does not involve continuous current.

subject: Science
notes: Heat is a form of energy that can be transferred from a hot body to a cold body.
Heat transfer occurs in three modes: conduction, convection and radiation.
Conduction is the transfer of heat through a solid material by molecular contact.
Conduction is fastest in metals like copper and slowest in insulators like plastic or wood.
Convection is the transfer of heat by the movement of a fluid (liquid or gas).
In convection hot fluid rises because it is less dense and cold fluid sinks.
Radiation is the transfer of heat through electromagnetic waves and does not need a medium.
The Sun’s heat reaches Earth mainly by radiation.
A thermometer measures temperature by the expansion of a liquid (mercury or alcohol).
Heat causes solids to expand and liquids to contract or expand when heated.
The expansion of metals is why railway tracks have gaps at the joints.
A thermos flask uses a vacuum and a silvered inner surface to reduce heat loss by conduction, convection and radiation.
White colour reflects more solar radiation, keeping objects cooler in summer.
Black colour absorbs more radiation, keeping objects warmer in winter.
Heat can be transferred by touching a hot object; the hotter the object, the faster the heat transfer.
Heat energy can be stored in hot water or in a hot metal spoon.
Heat transfer can be observed in everyday life: boiling water, ice melting, sunlight warming a room, etc.

quiz.q: Which mode of heat transfer does not require a medium?
quiz.explain: Radiation can transfer heat through empty space.

quiz.q: In the experiment with copper, steel, and aluminium bars, which bar caused the pins to fall first?
options: All fell at the same time
quiz.explain: Copper conducts heat fastest, so pins fall first.

quiz.q: What happens to water density when it is heated?
quiz.explain: Heating reduces water density, causing it to rise.

quiz.q: Why do we wear woolen clothes in winter?
quiz.explain: Wool insulates and retains body heat.

quiz.q: Which substance is a good conductor of heat?
quiz.explain: Copper conducts heat well.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the vacuum in a thermos flask?
quiz.explain: Vacuum stops heat transfer by conduction and convection.

quiz.q: Which of the following causes sea breezes?
quiz.explain: Sea breezes are created by convection currents.

quiz.q: Why are houses in Rajasthan painted white?
quiz.explain: White paint reflects sunlight, reducing heat absorption.

quiz.q: Which gas expands when heated?
quiz.explain: All gases expand when heated.

quiz.q: What is the effect of black paint on a metal tin exposed to sunlight?
quiz.explain: Black paint absorbs more radiation, increasing temperature.

subject: Science
notes: सजीवांमध्ये विविधता का असते? – वातावरणाशी जुळवून घेण्यासाठी अनुकूलन (Adaptation) होते.
अनुकूलन म्हणजे सजीवांच्या शरीरातील अवयव व जीवनशैलीत होणारे बदल, ज्यामुळे ते आपल्या परिसरात टिकून राहू शकतात.
वनस्पतींची अनुकूलने: पाण्यात तरंगणारी पाने, मेणचट थर, जाड साली, बर्फ साचू न देणारी शंकूची रचना, खोल मुळे.
वाळवंटी वनस्पतींची अनुकूलने: पातळ पाने, काटे, मांसल खोड, पाण्याचे साठवण, पाण्याचे कमी वाफेचे रूपांतर.
हिमप्रदेशातील वनस्पतींची अनुकूलने: शंकूची रचना, जाड साली, बर्फ साचू न देणारी फांद्या.
जंगलातील वनस्पतींची अनुकूलने: उंच खोड, स्पर्धा, वेलींची वाढ.
गवताळ प्रदेशातील वनस्पतींची अनुकूलने: तंतुमय मुळे, धूप रोखणे, प्रकाश मिळवण्यासाठी उंच वाढ.

प्राण्यांची अनुकूलने: पाण्यातील प्राण्यांची त्वचा खवले, पंख, पायांवरील पडदे; उभयचरांची पायांची बोटे, त्वचेचे श्वसन; मांसाहारी प्राण्यांचे तीक्ष्ण सुळे, चोच; शाकाहारी प्राण्यांचे मोठे डोळे, पायांचे बारीकपणा.
अनुकूलनाचे प्रकार: शारीरिक (आकार, रंग), शारीरिक रचना (पंख, खवले), वर्तनात्मक (शिकार पद्धती).
डार्विनचा सिद्धान्त: ज्या सजीवांना अनुकूलन असते ते टिकतात, पुढच्या पिढीत ती वैशिष्ट्ये वारसाहक्काने मिळतात.
वर्गीकरण: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. प्रत्येक पातळीवर वैशिष्ट्ये वेगळी असतात.
दुहेरी नाव पद्धती (Binomial nomenclature): प्रजाती व जातीची नावे, उदाहरण: Homo sapiens.
अनुकूलनाचे महत्त्व: अन्न मिळवणे, पाणी व ऊर्जा वाचवणे, शत्रूपासून संरक्षण.
अनुकूलनाचे निरीक्षण: आपल्या परिसरातील वनस्पती व प्राणी पाहून त्यांच्या अवयवांतील बदल नोंदवा.
अनुकूलनाचे उदाहरण: उंटाची जाड त्वचा व पायांची गादी, पांढरे केस, बर्फाळ प्रदेशातील प्राण्यांचे दाट केस.
अनुकूलन व उत्क्रांती यांचा संबंध: अनुकूलनामुळे प्रजातींची उत्क्रांती होते.
अनुकूलनाचे विविध प्रकार: शारीरिक, शारीरिक रचना, वर्तनात्मक, पर्यावरणीय.
अनुकूलनाचे महत्त्व: सजीवांना त्यांच्या अधिवासात टिकून राहण्यासाठी.
अनुकूलनाचे निरीक्षण व नोंदणी: प्रयोग, निरीक्षण तक्ता, प्रश्नोत्तरे.

quiz.q: वनस्पतींमध्ये पाण्याच्या पृष्ठभागावर तरंगण्यासाठी पोकळ्या असलेल्या अवयवाला काय म्हणतात?
quiz.explain: पाण्याच्या पृष्ठभागावर तरंगण्यासाठी पोकळ्या असलेल्या खोडाला पोकळ खोड म्हणतात.

quiz.q: वाळवंटी प्रदेशातील वनस्पतींच्या पानांचे स्वरूप कसे असते?
quiz.explain: वाळवंटी वनस्पतींमध्ये पानं सुईसारखी बारीक असतात.

quiz.q: हिमप्रदेशातील देवदार वृक्षाचे फांद्यांचे स्वरूप काय आहे?
quiz.explain: देवदार वृक्षाच्या फांद्या उतरत्या असतात.

quiz.q: अमरवेलीला अन्न मिळवण्यासाठी कोणत्या प्रकारचे मुळे असतात?
quiz.explain: अमरवेलीला अन्न शोषण्यासाठी चूषक मुळे असतात.

quiz.q: जंगलातील प्राण्यांच्या पायांच्या तळव्यांना काय वैशिष्ट्य असते?
quiz.explain: वाघाच्या पायांच्या तळव्यांना गादीसारखे असते.

quiz.q: पक्ष्यांच्या पंखांमध्ये काय वैशिष्ट्य असते ज्यामुळे ते हलके होतात?
quiz.explain: पक्ष्यांच्या पंखांमध्ये पोकळ हाडे असतात.

quiz.q: सरपटणाऱ्या प्राण्यांच्या त्वचेची वैशिष्ट्ये काय आहेत?
quiz.explain: सापाची त्वचा खवलेयुक्त असते.

quiz.q: भुचर प्राण्यांच्या पाठीचा कणा कशासाठी उपयुक्त असतो?
quiz.explain: पाठीचा कणा शिकार शोधण्यासाठी उपयुक्त असतो.

quiz.q: वाळवंटी प्राण्यांच्या त्वचेचे वैशिष्ट्य काय आहे?
quiz.explain: वाळवंटी प्राण्यांची त्वचा जाड असते.

quiz.q: सजीवांच्या वर्गीकरणात 'किंगडम' म्हणजे काय?
quiz.explain: किंगडम म्हणजे 'राज्य'.

subject: Science
notes: दुष्काळ म्हणजे पाणी व अन्नधान्याचा दीर्घकाळ तुटवडा होणे.
दुष्काळाचे दोन प्रकार – सौम्य दुष्काळ व तीव्र दुष्काळ.
दुष्काळाचे प्रमुख कारण अवर्षण (पर्जन्यमान कमी होणे).
मानवी कारणे: युद्ध, लोकसंख्या वाढ, जलसंधारणाचा अभाव.
पर्जन्यमान व लोकसंख्या यांचा समतोल बिघडल्यास पाण्याचा तुटवडा वाढतो.
पाण्याचा गैरबापर व वृक्षतोडीमुळे धूप व दुष्काळ वाढतो.
पाण्याचा नियोजनपूर्वक वापर व जलसंधारणाने दुष्काळ कमी होतो.
ढगफुटी म्हणजे ढगात साठलेले पाणी अचानक जमिनीवर पडणे.
महापूर म्हणजे मोठ्या प्रमाणात पाणी वाहून येणे, ज्यामुळे इमारती व वाहतूक प्रभावित होते.
बीज पडणे म्हणजे विजेचा आघात, 95% विजा आकाशातच राहतात.
विजेपासून जीवितहानी टाळण्यासाठी उंच ठिकाणे व विजेचे खांब टाळा.
ज्वालामुखीमुळे राख, उष्ण चिखल व वायू बाहेर पडतात, ज्यामुळे वातावरण प्रदूषित होते.
भूकंप व ज्वालामुखीचे उद्रेक महासागरात त्सुनामी लाट निर्माण करतात.
त्सुनामीची उंची 100 फूटापर्यंत जाऊ शकते व किनारी भागात मोठी हानी होते.
आपत्ती व्यवस्थापनात तात्काळ सूचना व आश्रय व्यवस्था महत्त्वाची.
सामाजिक व पर्यावरणीय संतुलन राखण्यासाठी वृक्षलागवड व जलसंधारण आवश्यक.
आपत्तीच्या वेळी सुरक्षित ठिकाण शोधणे व तात्काळ पळून जाणे गरजेचे.
आपत्ती व्यवस्थापनात राष्ट्रीय व स्थानिक स्तरावर आराखडा तयार करणे आवश्यक.
आपत्तीच्या वेळी मोबाइल व विद्युत उपकरणे वापरणे टाळणे सुरक्षित.
आपत्ती व्यवस्थापनात आंतरराष्ट्रीय मदत व स्वयंसेवकांची भूमिका महत्त्वाची.
आपत्तीच्या वेळी घरातील तारे व विजेचे खांब टाळणे सुरक्षित.
आपत्तीच्या वेळी पाण्याच्या स्रोतांची तपासणी व स्वच्छता आवश्यक.
आपत्तीच्या वेळी तात्काळ आपत्कालीन सेवा क्रमांकावर कॉल करणे आवश्यक.

quiz.q: दुष्काळाचे प्रमुख कारण काय आहे?
quiz.explain: दुष्काळाचे मुख्य कारण अवर्षण म्हणजे पर्जन्यमान कमी होणे.

quiz.q: विजेचा 95% भाग कुठे पडतो?
quiz.explain: विजेचे 95% आकाशातच राहते.

quiz.q: त्सुनामीची उंची साधारण किती असते?
quiz.explain: त्सुनामीची उंची सुमारे 100 फूट असू शकते.

quiz.q: ज्वालामुखीमुळे कोणते रासायनिक पदार्थ वातावरणात येतात?
quiz.explain: ज्वालामुखीमुळे राख व गंधक वायू वातावरणात येतात.

quiz.q: महापूराचे मुख्य परिणाम काय आहेत?
quiz.explain: महापूरामुळे इमारती व पायाभूत सुविधा नष्ट होतात.

quiz.q: दुष्काळ टाळण्यासाठी काय करावे?
quiz.explain: पाण्याचा नियोजनपूर्वक वापर दुष्काळ कमी करतो.

quiz.q: विजेच्या वेळी कोणते ठिकाण सुरक्षित असते?
quiz.explain: पक्के घर सर्वात सुरक्षित ठिकाण आहे.

quiz.q: त्सुनामीची ऊर्जा कुठून येते?
quiz.explain: त्सुनामीची ऊर्जा भूकंपामुळे महासागरात पाण्याला ढकलते.

quiz.q: विजेपासून जीवितहानी टाळण्यासाठी काय करावे?
quiz.explain: पक्के घरात राहणे सुरक्षित आहे.

quiz.q: ज्वालामुखीच्या उद्रेकानंतर काय होते?
quiz.explain: ज्वालामुखीच्या उद्रेकानंतर राख व वायू बाहेर पडतात.

subject: Science
notes: सजीवांचे शरीर सूक्ष्म घटकांनी बनलेले असते ज्याला पेशी म्हणतात.
पेशी ही सजीवांची मूलभूत रचनात्मक व कार्यात्मक एकक आहे.
सर्व सजीव पेशींच्या पातळीवर कार्य करतात – पेशी, ऊती, अवयव, अवयवसंस्था.
एकपेशीय सजीवांच्या जीवनक्रिया पेशीमध्येच घडतात.
रॉबर्ट हुक यांनी १६६५ साली सूक्ष्मदर्शकाखाली पेशी शोधल्या आणि त्यांना 'सेला' (लहान खोली) असे नाव दिले.
श्लायडेन व श्वान यांनी १८३८ साली पेशी सिद्धान्त मांडला – सर्व सजीव पेशींपासून बनलेले आहेत.
विरशॉ यांनी १८८५ साली सांगितले की नवीन पेशी पूर्वीच्या पेशींमधूनच जन्म घेतात.
पेशींचे मोजमाप मायक्रोमीटर व नॅनोमीटर या एककांनी केले जाते.
संयुक्‍त सूक्ष्मदर्शकात वस्तू १००० पटीने मोठी दिसते.
वनस्पती पेशींच्या भोवती पेशीभित्तिका असते, प्राणी पेशींच्या भोवती पेशीपटल असते.
पेशीपटल लवचिक व नाजूक असते, पेशीभित्तिका कठीण व स्थिर असते.
पेशीतील द्रव भागाला पेशीद्रव म्हणतात, ज्यात अंगके विखुरलेली असतात.
केंद्रक हे पेशीचे सर्वात महत्त्वाचे अंगक असून दुहेरी पटल असते.
आंतररट्रव्यजालिका प्रथिनांचे बदल करून गॉल्जीपिंडाकडे पाठवते.
गॉल्जीपिंड चपट्या पिशव्यांनी बनलेले असते, प्रथिनांचे वितरण करते.
तंतुकणिका ऊर्जा तयार करते – पेशीचे ऊर्जाकेंद्र, प्राणी व वनस्पती दोन्हीमध्ये असते.
वनस्पती पेशींमध्ये हरितलवके प्रकाशसंश्लेषण करतात, प्राणी पेशींमध्ये रिक्तिका लहान असते.
सूक्ष्मजीव म्हणजे डोळ्यांनी न दिसणारे सजीव, ज्यांना सूक्ष्मदर्शकाने पाहतात.
सूक्ष्मजीवांचे वर्गीकरण एकपेशीय (उदा. अमीबा, जीवाणू) व बहुपेशीय (उदा. बुरशी) असे होते.
सूक्ष्मजीव अन्न, पाणी, माती, कचरा इत्यादी ठिकाणी आढळतात.
किण्वन म्हणजे सूक्ष्मजीवांच्या क्रियेने कार्बनी पदार्थांचे दुसऱ्या पदार्थात रूपांतर होणे.
प्रतिजैविके सूक्ष्मजीवांनी बनवली जातात आणि रोगजंतूंचा नाश करतात.
किण्वनाने पाव, इडली, दही इत्यादी पदार्थ हलके व फुगतात.
काळजीपूर्वक कचरा व्यवस्थापनाने सूक्ष्मजीवांच्या उपयुक्ततेचा लाभ घेतला जाऊ शकतो.
काळजी न घेतल्यास सूक्ष्मजीवांमुळे अन्नविषबाधा व रोग होऊ शकतात.

quiz.q: पेशीभित्तिका फक्त कोणत्या पेशींमध्ये आढळते?
quiz.explain: पेशीभित्तिका फक्त वनस्पती पेशींमध्ये असते.

quiz.explain: रिक्तिका वनस्पती पेशींमध्ये मोठी असते.

quiz.q: सूक्ष्मजीवांची वाढ व प्रजननासाठी काय आवश्यक असते?
quiz.explain: बहुतेक सूक्ष्मजीवांना ऑक्सिजन व पाणी दोन्ही आवश्यक असतात, परंतु काही ऑक्सिजनशिवायही वाढतात.

quiz.q: पेशींच्या संरक्षणासाठी काय मदत करते?
quiz.explain: पेशीपटल हे प्राणी पेशींचे संरक्षण करणारे आवरण आहे.

quiz.q: सूक्ष्मजीवांच्या निरीक्षणासाठी कोणता सूक्ष्मदर्शक वापरला जातो?
quiz.explain: संयुक्‍त सूक्ष्मदर्शक व इलेक्ट्रॉन सूक्ष्मदर्शक दोन्ही वापरले जातात.

quiz.explain: किण्वन हे सूक्ष्मजीवांच्या क्रियेने कार्बनी पदार्थांचे दुसऱ्या कार्बनी पदार्थांत रूपांतर होणे.

quiz.q: प्रतिजैविके कोणत्या जीवांपासून बनवली जातात?
quiz.explain: प्रतिजैविके बॅक्टेरियांच्या मदतीने बनवली जातात.

quiz.q: पेशीतील कोणते अंगक ऊर्जा निर्मिती करते?
quiz.explain: तंतुकणिका (माइटोकॉन्ड्रिया) ऊर्जा निर्मितीचे कार्य करते.

subject: Science
notes: स्नायू म्हणजे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण करणारे तंतूंचे समूह.
मानवी शरीरात 600 पेक्षा जास्त स्नायू असून ते शरीराच्या 40% वजनाचे असतात.
स्नायूंचे तीन प्रकार: अस्थी (स्नायू), हृदयाचे, आणि गुळगुळीत (स्मूथ) स्नायू.
अस्थी स्नायू दोन हाडांना जोडलेले असतात व हालचाल ऐच्छिक असते.
हृदयाचे स्नायू अनैच्छिक असून दर मिनिटाला 70 वेळा आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण करतात.
गुळगुळीत स्नायू जठर, आतडे, रक्तवाहिन्या व गर्भाशयात आढळतात व हालचाल सावकाश व आपोआप असते.
स्नायूंचे आकुंचन शरीराला विशिष्ट स्थिती व हालचाल देतात.
स्नायू व हाडे स्नायुबंधांनी जोडलेले असतात.
स्नायूंची आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण एकमेकांना पूरक असतात.
स्नायूंचे कार्य: आकुंचन, शिथिलीकरण, शरीराची स्थिती राखणे.
स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण शरीराच्या सर्व भागांत होते.
स्नायूंचे कार्य शरीराच्या वाढीसोबत वाढते.
स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण शरीरातील विविध क्रिया नियंत्रित करतात.
स्नायूंचे कार्य शरीराच्या विविध अवयवांमध्ये वेगवेगळे असते.
स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण शरीराच्या आरोग्यासाठी अत्यावश्यक आहे.

quiz.q: स्नायूंचे तीन मुख्य प्रकार कोणते?
quiz.explain: स्नायूंचे तीन प्रकार अस्थी, हृदयाचे व गुळगुळीत (स्मूथ) आहेत.

quiz.q: हृदयाचे स्नायू कोणत्या प्रकारचे असतात?
quiz.explain: हृदयाचे स्नायू अनैच्छिक असतात.

quiz.q: स्नायू व हाडे कसे जोडलेले असतात?
quiz.explain: स्नायू व हाडे स्नायुबंधांनी जोडलेले असतात.

quiz.q: स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण शरीरात काय करते?
quiz.explain: स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण शरीराला स्थिती व हालचाल देते, रक्ताभिसरण व पचनास मदत करते.

quiz.q: स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण कोणत्या अवयवात सर्वाधिक होते?
quiz.explain: हृदयात दर मिनिटाला सुमारे 70 वेळा आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण होते.

quiz.q: स्नायूंचा मुख्य कार्य काय आहे?
quiz.explain: स्नायूंचे मुख्य कार्य हालचाल व स्थिती राखणे आहे.

quiz.q: गुळगुळीत स्नायू कोणत्या अवयवात आढळतात?
quiz.explain: गुळगुळीत स्नायू जठर, आतडे व रक्तवाहिन्यांमध्ये आढळतात.

quiz.q: स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण कसे होते?
quiz.explain: स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण नर्व्ह सिग्नलने होते.

quiz.q: स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण शरीराच्या कोणत्या भागात सर्वाधिक असते?
quiz.explain: हृदयात सर्वाधिक आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण होते.

quiz.q: स्नायूंचे आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरण शरीरात कसे समन्वयित असते?
options: एकाच वेळी सर्व स्नायू आकुंचन करतात
एकाच वेळी सर्व स्नायू शिथिल होतात
quiz.explain: स्नायूंचे गट एकमेकांना पूरक असतात व समन्वयित काम करतात.

subject: Science
notes: बदल म्हणजे एखाद्या पदार्थाचे गुणधर्म किंवा स्वरूप बदलणे.
भौतिक बदलात पदार्थाचे रूप बदलते पण रासायनिक संघटन तसंच राहते (उदा. पाण्याचे बाष्पीभवन).
रासायनिक बदलात पदार्थाचे रासायनिक संघटन बदलते, नवीन पदार्थ तयार होतो (उदा. लोखंडाचे गंजणे).
निसर्गनिर्मित बदल म्हणजे निसर्गात स्वतःहून होणारे बदल (फळ पिकणे, पाऊस पडणे).
मानवनिर्मित बदल म्हणजे मानवाने केलेले बदल (भाजी चिरणे, भाकरी भाजणे).
उपयुक्त बदल म्हणजे मानवाला उपयोगी पडणारे बदल (उदा. अन्न शिजवणे).
हानिकारक बदल म्हणजे मानवाला हानी पोहोचवणारे बदल (उदा. लोखंड गंजणे).
परिवर्तनीय बदल म्हणजे उलट सुलट होऊ शकणारे बदल (उदा. मेणबत्ती वितळणे आणि पुन्हा मेण बनवणे).
अपरिवर्तनीय बदल म्हणजे एकदा झाल्यावर परत येऊ न शकणारे बदल (उदा. पिकलेल्या आंब्याचे पुन्हा आंबे होणे).
आवर्ती बदल म्हणजे ठराविक कालावधीनंतर पुन्हा होणारे बदल (उदा. पाऊस, सूर्यप्रकाश).
अनावर्ती बदल म्हणजे एकदा झाल्यावर पुन्हा होण्याची खात्री नसलेले बदल (उदा. भूकंप).
भौतिक बदलाचे उदाहरण: पाण्याचे बाष्पीभवन, वस्तू फुटणे, द्रवाचे अवस्थांतर.
रासायनिक बदलाचे उदाहरण: लोखंडाचे गंजणे, दुधाचे दही होणे, साखरेचे जळणे.
भौतिक बदलात पदार्थाचे गुणधर्म बदलतात पण रासायनिक सूत्र तसंच राहते. रासायनिक बदलात नवीन रासायनिक सूत्र तयार होते.
बदलाचे वर्गीकरण करताना बदलाचे कारण, कालावधी, परिणाम, आणि पदार्थाचे रूप बदलते का हे लक्षात घ्यावे.

quiz.q: बदल म्हणजे काय?
quiz.explain: बदल म्हणजे पदार्थाचे गुणधर्म किंवा स्वरूप बदलणे.

quiz.q: खालीलपैकी कोणता बदल नैसर्गिक बदल आहे?
quiz.explain: फळ पिकणे हे नैसर्गिक बदल आहे.

quiz.q: मानवनिर्मित बदलाचे उदाहरण कोणते?
quiz.explain: भाजी चिरणे हे मानवनिर्मित बदल आहे.

quiz.q: भौतिक बदलाचे उदाहरण कोणते?
quiz.explain: पाण्याचे बाष्पीभवन भौतिक बदल आहे.

quiz.q: रासायनिक बदलाचे उदाहरण कोणते?
quiz.explain: लोखंड गंजणे रासायनिक बदल आहे.

quiz.q: खालीलपैकी कोणता बदल शीघ्र होणारा बदल आहे?
quiz.explain: फुगा फुटणे शीघ्र होणारा बदल आहे.

quiz.q: काय बदल आवर्ती बदल म्हणतात?
quiz.explain: आवर्ती बदलांचे कालावधी निश्चित असतो.

quiz.q: काय बदल अनावर्ती बदल म्हणतात?
quiz.explain: अनावर्ती बदलांचे कालावधी अनिश्चित असतो.

quiz.q: बदलांचे वर्गीकरण करताना कोणते निकष विचारात घ्यावेत?
quiz.explain: सर्व निकष विचारात घ्यावेत.

quiz.q: भौतिक बदलात नवीन पदार्थ तयार होत नाही, हे बरोबर आहे का?
quiz.explain: भौतिक बदलात नवीन पदार्थ तयार होत नाही.

subject: Science
notes: पदार्थ म्हणजे सर्व वस्तू ज्यापासून बनलेल्या असतात. द्रव्य हेच पदार्थाचे वैज्ञानिक नाव आहे.
पदार्थाचे तीन अवस्था: स्थायू (घन), द्रव, वायू. या अवस्थांमध्ये द्रव्याचे गुणधर्म बदलतात पण कण समान राहतात.
पदार्थाचे मुख्य गुणधर्म: वस्तुमान, आकारमान, रंग, सुवास, घनता, उष्णताबाहकता, विद्युतवाहकता, तन्यता, धातू/अधातू गुणधर्म.
मूलद्रव्य हे एकच प्रकारचे अणू असलेले पदार्थ. उदाहरण: हायड्रोजन, ऑक्सिजन, लोह.
संयुग हे दोन किंवा अधिक मूलद्रव्यांचे रासायनिक संयोग. रेणू म्हणजे संयुगाचे लहान कण.
मिश्रण हे दोन किंवा अधिक पदार्थांचे भौतिक मिश्रण. मिश्रणात रासायनिक बदल होत नाही.
मिश्रणांचे वर्ग: समरूप (homogeneous) आणि विषम (heterogeneous).
मिश्रणातील घटक वेगळे करण्याच्या पद्धती: गाळणे, चाळणे, चुंबक फिरवणे, उर्ध्वपातन, अपकेंद्रीकरण, रंजकद्रव्य पृथक्करण.
धातूंचे गुणधर्म: चकाकी, तन्यता, विद्युतवाहकता, उष्णताबाहकता. अधातूंचे गुणधर्म: कमी चकाकी, कमी तन्यता, कमी विद्युतवाहकता.
धातुसदृश (alloy) म्हणजे दोन किंवा अधिक धातूंचे मिश्रण ज्यात धातूंचे गुणधर्म बदलतात.
मूलद्रव्यांच्या संज्ञा इंग्रजी अक्षरांच्या संक्षिप्त रूपात लिहिल्या जातात (H, O, Na, Mg इ.).
मूलद्रव्यांचे शोध वर्ष आणि अवस्था तक्त्यात नोंदवली जाते.
मिश्रणांचे उदाहरण: मीठ, भेळ, सरबत, पाणी, दूध, गढूळ पाणी.
संयुगांचे उदाहरण: पाणी (H₂O), मीठ (NaCl), सल्फ्युरिक आम्ल (H₂SO₄).
मिश्रणातील घटक वेगळे करण्यासाठी उष्णता, चुंबक, गाळणी, अपकेंद्रीकरण इ. पद्धती वापरतात.

notes: नैसर्गिक पदार्थ म्हणजे पृथ्वीवरून मिळणारे पदार्थ जसे की पाणी, हवा, खडक इ.
मानवनिर्मित पदार्थ म्हणजे मानवाने तयार केलेले पदार्थ जसे की टूथपेस्ट, साबण, सिमेंट इ.
दात स्वच्छ करण्यासाठी आज टूथपेस्ट आणि टूथपावडर वापरतात. त्यातील प्रमुख घटक कॅल्शियम कार्बोनेट, फ्लोराइड इ.
फ्लोराइड दातांच्या आवरणाला मजबूत करते व दंतक्षय रोखते.
साबण हे तेलाम्लांचे सोडियम किंवा पोटॅशियम क्षार असते. ते पाण्यात मळ काढून टाकते.
साबणाची पृष्ठसक्रियता म्हणजे पृष्ठभागावर पसरून फेस तयार करण्याची क्षमता.
निसर्गनिर्मित अपमार्जकांमध्ये रिठा व शिकेकाई यांचा समावेश होतो. त्यात सॅपोनिन असते.
मानवनिर्मित संश्लिष्ट अपमार्जकांमध्ये सुगंध, रंग व जंतुनाशके असतात. ते कठीण पाण्यातही वापरता येतात.
सिमेंट हे सिलिका, अॅल्युमिना, चुना व आयर्न ऑक्साइड यांच्यापासून बनते. पोर्टलंड सिमेंटमध्ये 60% चुना असतो.
सिमेंट व पाणी, वाळू व खडी मिसळून काँक्रीट तयार होते. काँक्रीट रस्ते व इमारतींमध्ये वापरले जाते.
कठीण पाणी म्हणजे पाण्यात खनिजे जास्त असणे ज्यामुळे साबण फेस तयार करत नाही.
पृष्ठसक्रियता म्हणजे साबणाचे पाणी व तेल दोन्हीला एकत्र आणण्याची क्षमता.
साबण व संश्लिष्ट अपमार्जकांमध्ये फरक असा की साबण नैसर्गिक तेल व चरबीपासून बनतो, तर संश्लिष्ट अपमार्जक रासायनिक पद्धतीने बनवले जातात.
सिमेंटच्या घटकांमध्ये सिलिका, अॅल्युमिना, चुना व आयर्न ऑक्साइड असतात.
सिमेंट व सिमेंटच्या वापराने इमारती व रस्ते मजबूत व टिकाऊ बनतात.
पाणी कठीण आहे का हे साबणचुऱ्याने तपासता येते – जर साबण फेस तयार करत नसेल तर पाणी कठीण असते.
दातांची स्वच्छता करण्यासाठी टूथपेस्टमध्ये फ्लोराइड व पॉलिश करणारे घटक असतात.
साबणाचे प्रकार: कठीण साबण (कपडे धुण्यासाठी), मृदू साबण (स्नानासाठी).
सिमेंटच्या उत्पादनात वाळू, चुनखडी व जिप्सम यांचा वापर होतो.
सिमेंट व काँक्रीट हे बांधकामात प्रमुख साहित्य आहेत.
सिमेंट व पाणी मिसळल्यावर ते कडक होऊन घन पदार्थ बनते.
सिमेंट व पाणी वाळू व खडीसह मिसळून स्लॅब व भिंती बनवतात.
सिमेंट व पाणी यांचा गुणोत्तर योग्य ठेवणे आवश्यक आहे.
