subject: Science
chapter: Living World and Classification of Microbes
notes: Hierarchy of classification: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
Biodiversity is the variety of life; classification helps organise it.
Carl Linnaeus (1735) introduced the binomial system: each species gets a two‑word Latin name (Genus species).
The binomial name uses only the first letter of the genus capitalised; species name is lowercase.
Whittaker’s five‑kingdom system (1969): Monera, Protista, Plantae, Fungi, Animalia.
Monera are prokaryotic unicellular organisms (bacteria and cyanobacteria).
Protista are mostly unicellular eukaryotes with a nucleus and membrane‑bound organelles.
Plantae are autotrophic eukaryotes that perform photosynthesis and have cell walls made of cellulose.
Fungi are heterotrophic eukaryotes that absorb nutrients; their cell walls contain chitin.
Animalia are heterotrophic eukaryotes that ingest food; they lack cell walls.
Microbes are classified by size: Viruses (10‑100 nm), Bacteria (0.5‑5 µm), Protozoa (≈10‑200 µm), Fungi (≈10‑100 µm), Algae (≈10‑100 µm).
Bacteria reproduce by binary fission; many can double every 20 min under ideal conditions.
Protozoa have diverse locomotion: pseudopodia, cilia, flagella; they can be free‑living or parasitic.
Fungi reproduce both sexually and asexually; many are saprotrophs that decompose dead matter.
Algae perform photosynthesis using chloroplasts; some are unicellular, others multicellular.
Viruses are not considered living organisms; they need a host cell to replicate and are visible only with an electron microscope.
Key terms: prokaryote, eukaryote, autotrophic, heterotrophic, saprotroph, parasitic, binary fission, chitin, cellulose.
Important facts: The five‑kingdom system is widely accepted; newer systems add more kingdoms or domains.
Merits of Whittaker’s system: simple, based on cell type and nutrition, easy for students to remember.
Demerits: Some organisms (e.g., protists) are grouped together despite large differences; it does not reflect evolutionary relationships fully.

quiz.q: Who introduced the binomial system of nomenclature?
quiz.explain: Linnaeus developed the two‑word Latin naming system.

quiz.q: Which kingdom contains organisms that have a cell wall made of chitin?
quiz.explain: Fungi have chitin in their cell walls.

quiz.q: What is the size range of bacteria?
quiz.explain: Bacteria are about 0.5 to 5 micrometres in size.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a mode of nutrition for fungi?
quiz.explain: Fungi are heterotrophic; they do not perform photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Viruses are best described as:
quiz.explain: Viruses are considered organisms at the edge of life.

quiz.q: Which kingdom includes organisms that perform photosynthesis using chloroplasts?
quiz.explain: Protists such as algae have chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between prokaryotes and eukaryotes?
quiz.explain: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus; eukaryotes have a membrane‑bound nucleus.

quiz.q: Which of the following organisms is a parasitic protozoan that causes malaria?
quiz.explain: Plasmodium vivax is a protozoan parasite that causes malaria.

quiz.q: Which kingdom is characterized by organisms that absorb nutrients from decaying matter?
quiz.explain: Fungi are saprotrophs that absorb nutrients from dead material.

quiz.q: Which classification criterion is NOT used by Whittaker?
quiz.explain: Whittaker’s system does not use DNA sequence.

subject: Science
notes: Cell is the basic unit of life.
There are two main types of cells: plant cells and animal cells.
Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose; animal cells lack a cell wall.
The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins and is selectively permeable.
Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
Isotonic solution: no net water movement; hypotonic: water enters the cell; hypertonic: water leaves the cell.
Cytoplasm is the fluid inside the cell that contains organelles; cytosol is the liquid part without organelles.
Nucleus contains DNA, nucleolus, and chromatin; it controls cell activities and heredity.
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) has rough (with ribosomes) and smooth (without ribosomes) regions; it synthesises proteins and lipids.
Golgi complex modifies, sorts, and packages proteins into vesicles for transport.
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes and break down waste and old organelles.
Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell, producing ATP through respiration.
Vacuoles store water, ions, and waste; plant vacuoles maintain turgor pressure.
Plastids (chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts) are double‑membrane organelles that store pigments or food.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis; chromoplasts contain carotenoids for colour; leucoplasts store starch.
Eukaryotic cells have membrane‑bound organelles and a nucleus; prokaryotic cells lack these and are smaller.
Cell membrane’s selective permeability maintains homeostasis.
Osmotic pressure is the force exerted by water movement across the membrane.
Mitochondria have inner folds called cristae that increase surface area for ATP production.
Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis; they can be free in cytoplasm or attached to rough ER.
The nucleus is surrounded by a double membrane with nuclear pores for transport.
Cell wall provides support and prevents excess water entry.
The cytoplasm is sticky and facilitates chemical reactions.
Plant cells usually have a large central vacuole; animal cells have smaller vacuoles or none.
The Golgi complex is sometimes called the cell’s packing department.

quiz.q: Which organelle is known as the "powerhouse" of the cell?
quiz.explain: Mitochondria produce ATP.

quiz.q: What is the main function of the cell wall in plant cells?
options: Provide support and prevent excess water entry
quiz.explain: Cell wall gives support and limits water entry.

quiz.q: Which process moves water from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration across a selectively permeable membrane?
quiz.explain: Osmosis is water movement.

quiz.q: The Golgi complex is best described as a:
quiz.explain: Golgi modifies and packages proteins.

quiz.q: Which organelle contains digestive enzymes that break down waste?
quiz.explain: Lysosomes digest waste.

quiz.q: In a hypotonic solution, a cell will:
quiz.explain: Water enters the cell.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of plastid?
quiz.explain: Mitochondrion is not a plastid.

quiz.q: The nucleus is surrounded by:
quiz.explain: Nucleus has a double membrane with pores.

quiz.q: Which organelle is involved in protein synthesis on its surface?
quiz.explain: Rough ER has ribosomes.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about red blood cells?
options: They have a thick cell wall
quiz.explain: RBCs lack mitochondria.

subject: Science
notes: - The human body is made of cells, tissues, organs, and organ systems.
- Life processes (growth, reproduction, respiration, circulation, excretion, sensation, movement) are carried out by organ systems.
- An organ system is a group of organs that work together to perform a specific function.
- Major organ systems: digestive, respiratory, circulatory, nervous, excretory, reproductive, skeletal, muscular, endocrine, immune.
- Respiration has three stages: external (inhalation/exhalation), internal (gas exchange in tissues), cellular (oxidation of glucose to produce ATP).
- The respiratory system includes nose, pharynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs, alveoli, diaphragm.
- The circulatory system includes heart, arteries, veins, capillaries; it transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste, and immune cells.
- The heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles; it pumps blood through systemic and pulmonary circuits.
- Arteries carry oxygenated blood away from the heart (except pulmonary artery); veins carry deoxygenated blood to the heart (except pulmonary vein).
- Capillaries are single‑cell‑thick vessels that allow exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste between blood and tissues.
- Blood is a fluid connective tissue composed of plasma (55%) and cells (45%): red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
- Red blood cells carry oxygen via hemoglobin; white blood cells defend the body; platelets help blood clotting.
- Blood groups (A, B, AB, O) and Rh factor (+/-) determine compatibility for transfusion.
- Blood pressure is measured as systolic/diastolic (e.g., 120/80 mmHg).
- Healthy blood pressure ranges: 90–119/60–79 mmHg; hypertension is >140/90 mmHg.
- Blood donation is safe for healthy adults 18–60 years, with adequate weight and health checks.
- The diaphragm and chest wall movements create negative pressure for inhalation and positive pressure for exhalation.
- The heart rate (beats per minute) is about 72–75 in a healthy adult at rest.
- Blood is continuously produced in the bone marrow and replaced every 4–5 months.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a major organ system?
quiz.explain: Skeletal is a system, not an organ.

quiz.q: What is the main function of the alveoli?
quiz.explain: Alveoli are tiny air sacs where O₂ and CO₂ are exchanged.

quiz.q: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood away from the heart?
quiz.explain: The aorta carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.

quiz.q: What is the role of platelets in blood?
quiz.explain: Platelets aggregate to form a clot at injury sites.

quiz.q: Which part of the respiratory system filters air before it reaches the lungs?
quiz.explain: The nose filters, warms, and humidifies inhaled air.

quiz.q: What does the systolic pressure represent?
quiz.explain: Systolic is the peak pressure during ventricular contraction.

quiz.q: Which blood group is the universal donor?
quiz.explain: Type O can donate to any group.

quiz.q: Where are red blood cells produced?
quiz.explain: RBCs are formed in the red bone marrow.

quiz.q: Which of these is a function of the circulatory system?
quiz.explain: Circulation transports oxygen and other substances.

quiz.q: What is the main gas exchanged in the alveoli?
quiz.explain: Oxygen is taken in and CO₂ is expelled in alveoli.

subject: Science
notes: Acid is a substance that tastes sour and gives hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water.
Base tastes bitter, feels slippery and gives hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in water.
Litmus paper: blue turns red in acid, red turns blue in base.
Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in base.
Methyl orange: orange in acid, yellow in base.
Universal indicator changes through many colours from red (acid) to green (neutral) to blue (base).
Acids are used in food (citric, acetic), industry (sulphuric, hydrochloric) and medicine (antacids).
Bases are used in soap, cleaning, neutralising acids and in industry (sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide).
Neutralisation: Acid + Base → Salt + Water. Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
Strong acids (HCl, H₂SO₄) are corrosive; weak acids (acetic, citric) are milder.
Indicators are substances that change colour when they encounter acid or base.
Natural indicators can be made from hibiscus, rose, turmeric, red cabbage, etc.
Baking soda (NaHCO₃) is a base; when added to fruit juice it produces bubbles (CO₂).
Acidic solutions turn blue litmus red; basic solutions turn red litmus blue.
The pH scale: 0–7 acidic, 7 neutral, 7–14 basic.
Acids react with metals to produce hydrogen gas.
Acids react with carbonates to release CO₂ and heat.
Bases react with acids to form salts and water.
Acids and bases are essential for life: stomach acid digests food, enzymes use pH.
Acidic soil can be neutralised by adding lime (Ca(OH)₂).
Safety: never taste or touch strong acids or bases; use gloves and goggles.

quiz.q: Which indicator turns pink in a basic solution?
quiz.explain: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and turns pink in base.

quiz.q: What colour does blue litmus paper change to when dipped in an acid?
quiz.explain: Blue litmus turns red in acidic solutions.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a weak acid?
quiz.explain: Acetic acid is a weak, organic acid.

quiz.q: Baking soda added to lemon juice produces bubbles because it reacts with the acid to release which gas?
quiz.explain: CO₂ is released in the reaction of baking soda with acid.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about strong acids?
options: They release H⁺ ions in water.
They are used only in food.
quiz.explain: Strong acids fully dissociate to give H⁺ ions.

quiz.q: What is the product of neutralisation of HCl with NaOH?
quiz.explain: Neutralisation gives salt (NaCl) and water.

quiz.q: Which natural indicator turns red when placed on an acidic solution?
quiz.explain: Hibiscus indicator paper turns red in acid.

quiz.q: Which of these is a base used in soap production?
quiz.explain: Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) is used in soap making.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT an indicator?
quiz.explain: Water does not change colour; it is not an indicator.

quiz.q: What happens when a strong acid is added slowly to water?
options: It heats up and may splash.
It turns blue litmus red instantly.
quiz.explain: Adding slowly prevents violent exothermic reaction and splashing.

subject: Science
notes: - A chemical change is a process where the original substance changes its composition and forms new substances with different properties.
- Physical changes alter appearance or state but the substance’s composition remains the same.
- Key signs of a chemical change: change in colour, taste, temperature, gas evolution, or formation of a precipitate.
- In a chemical reaction, reactants are on the left side of the arrow and products on the right.
- The arrow in a chemical equation points from reactants to products.
- A word equation uses the names of substances; a chemical equation uses their formulas.
- Neutralisation is a type of chemical reaction where an acid reacts with a base to form a salt and water.
- Combustion is a fast, irreversible chemical change where a substance reacts with oxygen to produce CO₂ and H₂O.
- Ionic bonds form between a metal cation and a non‑metal anion; the metal donates electrons and the non‑metal accepts them.
- Covalent bonds form when two non‑metal atoms share electrons to complete their valence shells.
- The valency of an atom is the number of bonds it can form; it equals the number of electrons it can lose, gain, or share.
- In ionic compounds, the magnitude of the ionic charge equals the valency.
- In covalent compounds, each shared pair of electrons counts as one bond for both atoms.
- The octet rule states that atoms tend to have eight electrons in their outer shell (or two for hydrogen).
- A precipitate is a solid that forms when two soluble salts react to produce an insoluble salt.
- Carbon dioxide is a common gas produced in many chemical changes, e.g., baking soda + lemon juice.
- Respiration is a natural chemical change where glucose reacts with oxygen to produce CO₂, H₂O, and energy.
- Photosynthesis is the reverse of respiration; plants convert CO₂ and H₂O into glucose and O₂ using sunlight.
- Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions; adding sodium carbonate precipitates CaCO₃ and MgCO₃, softening the water.
- Chemical changes can be written in a balanced equation by ensuring atoms and charge are conserved.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of a chemical change?
options: The substance turns from solid to liquid
quiz.explain: Gas evolution indicates a new substance is formed.

quiz.q: What is the word equation for the reaction of baking soda with lemon juice?
options: Sodium bicarbonate + Citric acid → Carbon dioxide + Sodium citrate
Sodium bicarbonate + Citric acid → Sodium chloride + Water
Sodium bicarbonate + Citric acid → Carbon dioxide + Water
Sodium bicarbonate + Citric acid → Calcium carbonate + Water
quiz.explain: Baking soda reacts with citric acid to produce CO₂ and sodium citrate.

quiz.q: In the combustion of a fuel, which element is the common reactant?
quiz.explain: All fuels contain carbon which reacts with oxygen.

quiz.q: Which type of bond involves the transfer of electrons from one atom to another?
quiz.explain: Ionic bonds form when electrons are transferred.

quiz.q: What is the product of the reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid?
quiz.explain: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a natural chemical change?
quiz.explain: Respiration involves chemical reactions.

quiz.q: In a chemical equation, what are the substances on the left side called?
quiz.explain: Reactants are the starting materials.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of a physical change?
options: Baking soda reacting with lemon juice
quiz.explain: Melting changes state but not composition.

quiz.q: What is the valency of chlorine in NaCl?
quiz.explain: Cl⁻ has a valency of 1.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of a fast chemical change?
quiz.explain: Fast changes are usually irreversible, e.g., combustion.

subject: Science
notes: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hot object to a cold one.
Heat is measured in Joules (SI) or calories (CGS); 1 cal = 4.18 J.
Temperature tells how hot or cold an object is; it is the average kinetic energy of its atoms.
Heat causes expansion of solids, liquids and gases; cooling causes contraction.
When heat is added to a substance, its temperature rises and it expands; when heat is removed, temperature falls and it contracts.
The specific heat (c) of a substance is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of it by 1 °C (J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹).
Heat required: Q = m c ΔT.
Heat sources: Sun, Earth (geothermal), chemical fuels, electrical energy, nuclear fission, air.
Heat transfer occurs by conduction, convection and radiation.
Conduction: heat flows through a solid by molecular collisions.
Convection: heat carried by moving fluid (liquid or gas).
Radiation: heat carried by electromagnetic waves; the Sun is the main source of radiation heat.
Heat and temperature are different: heat is energy content, temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy.
Thermometers measure temperature; mercury or alcohol thermometers use liquid expansion, clinical thermometers use sensors.
Linear expansion: ΔL = α L₀ ΔT; α is linear expansion coefficient (1/°C).
Area expansion: ΔA = β A₀ ΔT; β ≈ 2α for solids.
Volume expansion: ΔV = γ V₀ ΔT; γ ≈ 3α for solids.
For gases, volume expands with temperature at constant pressure: V = V₀(1+β ΔT).
Density of a gas decreases when it is heated because its volume increases.
The expansion of railway rails and bridges is accommodated by gaps to avoid damage.
Heat can be measured using a calorimeter, which is thermally isolated and contains a known mass of water.
The final temperature in a calorimeter can be found by energy balance: Q₁+Q₂+Q₃=0.
The specific heat of a substance can be found if the masses, temperatures and final temperature are known.
Heat can be generated by chemical reactions (combustion) or by electrical heating.
Heat can also be produced by nuclear fission in atomic energy projects.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the largest natural source of heat on Earth?
quiz.explain: The Sun is the primary source of heat energy for Earth.

quiz.q: Heat is transferred by which of the following processes?
quiz.explain: Heat can be transferred by conduction, convection, or radiation.

quiz.q: The unit of heat in the SI system is
quiz.explain: Heat is measured in joules in SI units.

quiz.q: One calorie is equivalent to how many joules?
When a hot object is placed in a cold one, what happens to their temperatures?
quiz.explain: Heat flows from hot to cold, so hot cools and cold warms.

quiz.q: Specific heat is defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of
quiz.explain: Specific heat c = Q/(mΔT) with m in kg and ΔT in °C.

quiz.q: Which thermometer type uses a liquid that expands with temperature?
quiz.explain: Alcohol thermometers use liquid expansion; mercury is hazardous.

quiz.q: At what temperature are Celsius and Fahrenheit equal?
quiz.explain: C = F when both are -40°.

quiz.q: The formula to convert Fahrenheit to Celsius is
Which of the following is NOT a source of heat?
quiz.explain: Electrical energy is a form of energy, not a source of heat per se.

subject: Science
notes: - Sound is produced when a vibrating object moves air molecules, creating alternating regions of compression and rarefaction.
- A tuning fork has two prongs; when struck, the prongs vibrate and set the surrounding air into waves.
- Compression = high pressure, high density; rarefaction = low pressure, low density.
- The vibration of the prongs is periodic; each complete forward‑backward motion is one cycle.
- One cycle of compression and rarefaction is called a wave cycle; the number of cycles per second is the frequency.
- Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz); 1 Hz = one cycle per second.
- A tuning fork of 512 Hz vibrates 512 times per second, producing 512 cycles of sound per second.
- The frequency of a sound depends on the vibrating object's size, shape, material and tension.
- In a glass cup experiment, the height of the air column determines the frequency; higher column → lower frequency.
- Musical notes are produced by changing the frequency of vibration (strings, air columns, vocal cords).
- Sound needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to propagate; in vacuum sound cannot travel.
- Loudspeakers convert electrical energy into mechanical vibration of a diaphragm, producing sound waves.
- Human voice is produced in the larynx where vocal cords vibrate as air passes through.
- Sound level is measured in decibels (dB); loud sounds above ~100 dB can be harmful.
- Sound intensity decreases with distance from the source; intensity ∝ 1/(distance²).

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a region in a sound wave?
quiz.explain: Amplitude is a property of the wave, not a region.

quiz.q: A tuning fork vibrates 512 times per second. What is its frequency?
quiz.explain: Frequency equals number of vibrations per second.

quiz.q: Sound can travel through a vacuum because:
options: Sound is a form of light
quiz.explain: Sound requires a medium; in vacuum it cannot propagate.

quiz.q: When the air column inside a glass cup is shortened, the frequency of the sound produced:
quiz.explain: Shorter column → higher frequency.

quiz.q: Which part of the human body produces sound when we speak?
quiz.explain: Vocal cords in the larynx vibrate to produce sound.

quiz.q: In a loudspeaker, the coil moves because:
options: It is magnetised by a permanent magnet
It is struck by a hammer
It is powered by a battery
quiz.explain: The coil is attracted/repelled by the magnetic field of the permanent magnet.

quiz.q: The distance between two vibrating points on a string is increased, the frequency:
quiz.explain: Longer vibrating length lowers the frequency.

quiz.q: Which of these is a correct statement about sound intensity?
options: It is the same as frequency
quiz.explain: Intensity falls as distance from source increases.

quiz.q: The region of a sound wave with higher pressure is called:
quiz.explain: Higher pressure region is compression.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a source of sound?
quiz.explain: Light bulb does not produce sound.

subject: Science
notes: Reflection of light is the change in direction of light rays when they strike a surface and bounce back.
The incident ray is the light ray that strikes the surface.
The point where the incident ray meets the surface is called the point of incidence.
The line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence is called the normal.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal is the angle of incidence (θi).
The ray after bouncing back is the reflected ray.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal is the angle of reflection (θr).
Law of reflection: θi = θr for all surfaces.
Regular (smooth) surfaces give parallel reflected rays; rough surfaces give scattered rays.
A plane mirror produces a virtual, upright, laterally reversed image that is the same size as the object.
The image in a mirror is formed on the same side of the mirror as the object, so left and right are swapped.
In water, light is reflected and then refracted; the reflected image is also inverted horizontally.
A kaleidoscope uses multiple reflections between mirrors to produce many images.
A periscope uses two mirrors at 45° to see over obstacles.
Light must be reflected or refracted to be seen; in darkness there is no light to reflect.
The laws of reflection hold even for irregular surfaces at each point of incidence.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection even when the ray is perpendicular to the surface (both 0°).

quiz.q: Which ray is called the incident ray?
options: The ray that leaves the surface
The ray that strikes the surface
quiz.explain: The incident ray is the one that strikes the surface.

quiz.q: What is the normal?
options: A line parallel to the surface
A line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence
quiz.explain: The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.

quiz.q: If the angle of incidence is 30°, what is the angle of reflection?
quiz.explain: By the law of reflection, θi = θr.

quiz.q: Which type of surface gives parallel reflected rays?
quiz.explain: Regular (smooth) surfaces give parallel reflected rays.

quiz.q: In a plane mirror, the image is
quiz.explain: A plane mirror gives a virtual, upright image.

quiz.q: What happens to left and right in a mirror image?
quiz.explain: The image is laterally reversed.

quiz.q: A periscope uses mirrors set at what angle to each other?
quiz.explain: Mirrors are set at 45° to each other.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a property of regular reflection?
quiz.explain: Regular reflection occurs on smooth surfaces.

quiz.q: Which phenomenon explains the many images seen in a kaleidoscope?
quiz.explain: Multiple reflections between mirrors create many images.

quiz.q: If a light ray is incident perpendicular to a mirror, the angle of incidence is
quiz.explain: Perpendicular incidence gives 0° angle with the normal.

subject: Science
notes: Manmade materials are those produced by humans from natural or synthetic substances.
Examples: glass, plastic, thermocol (polystyrene), artificial threads, rubber, metal alloys.
Plastic is a polymer made of long chains of molecules; it can be linear or branched.
Thermoplastic can be reshaped when heated and re-solidified when cooled (e.g., PVC, PS, PE, PP).
Thermosetting plastic hardens permanently after the first heat treatment; it cannot be remolded (e.g., Bakelite, melamine).
Properties of plastic: non‑corrosive, non‑decomposing, light, mouldable, poor conductor of heat and electricity.
Thermocol (polystyrene) melts above 100 °C and returns to solid on cooling; used for packaging and disposable plates.
Glass is a non‑crystalline solid made mainly of silica (SiO₂) with additives; it is transparent, brittle, and a good electrical insulator.
Types of glass: silica, borosilicate, alkali‑silicate, lead, optical, coloured, processed.
Soda‑lime glass is the most common type; it is made by melting sand, soda, and lime at ~1500 °C.
Glass is non‑degradable and can release harmful gases if burned; it is recyclable but takes long to degrade naturally.
Environmentally, plastics are often non‑degradable; biodegradable alternatives include jute, cotton, paper bags, and certain plastics like biodegradable polymers.
The 4 R principle: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover – helps minimise plastic waste.
Thermosetting plastics are used where permanent strength is needed (e.g., electrical switches, radio cabinets).
Thermoplastics are used for items that need moulding and re‑use (e.g., bottles, toys).
Thermocol is a form of polystyrene; it is a good shock absorber but can release carcinogenic styrene if heated.
Glass can be coloured by adding metal oxides (e.g., copper for red glass, iron for green).
In vehicles, safety glass (tempered or laminated) is used to prevent injury in accidents.
Plastic production involves polymerisation of monomers, extrusion, moulding, and sometimes additive blending.
Glass production involves melting raw materials, controlling temperature, and rapid cooling to avoid crystallisation.
Both plastic and glass can be recycled; recycling reduces raw material consumption and pollution.
Proper disposal of plastic and glass reduces environmental impact and protects human health.

quiz.q: Which type of plastic can be reshaped when heated and re‑solidified when cooled?
quiz.explain: Thermoplastics soften on heating and harden on cooling.

quiz.q: What is the main component of soda‑lime glass?
quiz.explain: Soda‑lime glass contains silica, soda, and lime.

quiz.q: Which glass type is used for laboratory glassware due to its low thermal expansion?
quiz.explain: Borosilicate glass has minimal thermal expansion.

quiz.q: Thermosetting plastic becomes permanently hard after the first heat treatment. Which example is correct?
quiz.explain: Bakelite is a thermosetting plastic.

quiz.q: Which property of plastic makes it a good shock absorber?
quiz.explain: Plasticity allows it to absorb shocks.

quiz.q: What temperature does thermocol (polystyrene) melt above?
quiz.explain: Thermocol melts above 100 °C.

quiz.q: Which metal oxide is added to glass to give it a blue‑green colour?
quiz.explain: Copper oxide gives blue‑green glass.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical use of thermoplastic PVC?
quiz.explain: PVC is not used for switches; it is used for insulation.

quiz.q: Which principle is used to reduce plastic waste?
quiz.explain: The 4R principle: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover.

quiz.q: Which glass type is soluble in water and is called 'water glass'?
quiz.explain: Alkali‑silicate glass dissolves in water.

subject: Science
notes: Biotic factors are living components of an ecosystem such as plants, animals, fungi and microbes.
Abiotic factors are non‑living components like air, water, soil, sunlight, temperature and minerals.
An ecosystem is the community of biotic and abiotic factors that interact and depend on each other.
Producers (autotrophs) use sunlight to make food through photosynthesis.
Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers.
Secondary consumers (carnivores or omnivores) eat primary consumers.
Tertiary consumers are top predators that eat secondary consumers.
Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead organic matter into inorganic substances.
The position of an organism in the food chain is called its trophic level.
Niche is the role an organism plays in its ecosystem, including its habitat and food source.
Biomes are large areas of land or water with similar climate and characteristic ecosystems, e.g., forest, grassland, desert, tundra, marine.
Grasslands develop where rainfall is insufficient for large trees and support grasses and grazing animals.
Evergreen forests have dense tree cover year‑round and support diverse wildlife.
Aquatic ecosystems include freshwater (ponds, rivers) and marine (oceans, seas).
Water currents transfer energy in aquatic ecosystems and support a different food web.
Decomposers recycle nutrients back into the soil or water, maintaining the cycle.
Human activities such as deforestation, mining, dam building, and pollution disturb ecosystems.
Urbanization replaces natural habitats with buildings and roads, reducing biodiversity.
Industrialization consumes forest resources and creates waste that harms ecosystems.
Tourism can damage ecosystems through litter, noise and habitat destruction.
Natural disasters like floods, droughts and earthquakes can alter or destroy ecosystems.
Conservation areas such as national parks protect key species and habitats.
Balancing human needs with ecosystem health is essential for long‑term sustainability.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a biotic factor?
quiz.explain: Plants are living organisms, hence biotic.

quiz.q: What process do producers use to make food?
quiz.explain: Producers convert sunlight into food via photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Which trophic level includes lions in a grassland?
quiz.explain: Lions are top predators, so tertiary consumers.

quiz.q: Decomposers convert organic matter into inorganic substances. Which group is NOT a decomposer?
quiz.explain: Plants are producers, not decomposers.

quiz.q: Which factor is abiotic?
quiz.explain: Sunlight is a non‑living abiotic factor.

quiz.q: A forest ecosystem is an example of which biome?
quiz.explain: Forest biomes contain forests.

quiz.q: Which human activity is most likely to cause loss of wetlands?
quiz.explain: Urbanization often converts wetlands into built land.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a primary consumer in a freshwater ecosystem?
quiz.explain: Insects eat algae, making them primary consumers.

quiz.q: What is the main role of a niche?
options: To describe an organism’s diet only
To describe an organism’s habitat only
To describe an organism’s role in its ecosystem
quiz.explain: A niche includes habitat, diet and role.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a type of aquatic ecosystem?
quiz.explain: Desert is terrestrial, not aquatic.

subject: Science
notes: - A galaxy is a huge collection of stars, planets and interstellar clouds. Our galaxy is a spiral galaxy called the Milky Way.
- The Sun is an ordinary star; it looks big because it is very close to us.
- Stars are gigantic spheres of hot gas, mainly hydrogen and helium.
- The mass of a star is usually expressed in solar masses (M☉).
- The radius of a star is measured in solar radii (R☉).
- The age of a star is the time since it formed; the Sun is about 4.5 billion years old.
- Stars are born from interstellar clouds that collapse under gravity.
- When the core temperature rises, hydrogen fuses into helium, producing energy and light.
- Stars stay in balance when inward gravitational force equals outward gas pressure.
- When the hydrogen fuel in the core is exhausted, the star expands into a red giant.
- Low‑mass stars (< 8 M☉) become white dwarfs after shedding their outer layers.
- Medium‑mass stars (8–25 M☉) become neutron stars after a supernova explosion.
- Very massive stars (> 25 M☉) collapse into black holes after the supernova.
- The life span of a star is inversely related to its mass – massive stars evolve faster.
- A light year is the distance light travels in one year (≈9.5 × 10¹⁵ m).
- The Sun will become a red giant in about 4–5 billion years, possibly swallowing Mercury and Venus.
- White dwarfs have Earth‑sized radii but very high densities; a spoonful would weigh several tons.
- Neutron stars are about 10 km in diameter but have densities so high that a spoonful would weigh the mass of all living beings on Earth.

quiz.q: Which type of galaxy contains a spiral shape with a central bulge and arms?
quiz.explain: Spiral galaxies have a disc with a central bulge and spiral arms.

quiz.q: What is the main source of energy for a main‑sequence star like the Sun?
quiz.explain: Main‑sequence stars generate energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.

quiz.q: What unit is used to measure very large distances in space?
quiz.explain: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, used for interstellar distances.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a constituent of a galaxy?
quiz.explain: Galaxies contain stars, planets, and interstellar material, but not human settlements.

quiz.q: What happens to a star after it exhausts hydrogen in its core and has a mass less than 8 times that of the Sun?
options: It turns into a black hole
quiz.explain: Low‑mass stars end as white dwarfs after the red‑giant phase.

quiz.q: The pressure that supports a white dwarf against gravity is mainly due to what?
quiz.explain: White dwarfs are supported by electron degeneracy pressure.

quiz.q: Which phenomenon occurs when a massive star (8–25 M☉) explodes at the end of its life?
quiz.explain: Stars in this mass range end as Type II supernovae, leaving neutron stars.

quiz.q: What is the approximate radius of a neutron star?
quiz.explain: Neutron stars are about 10 km in radius.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes the stability of a star?
options: Balance between gravitational force and gas pressure
Balance between magnetic and electric forces
Balance between nuclear and gravitational forces
quiz.explain: A star is stable when inward gravity balances outward gas pressure.

quiz.q: The Sun will become a red giant after roughly how many years?
quiz.explain: The Sun is expected to enter the red‑giant phase in about 4–5 billion years.

subject: Science
notes: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well‑being, not just absence of disease.
A disease is a disturbance in normal physiological or psychological processes of the body.
Diseases are classified by duration: acute (short) or chronic (long).
They are also classified by cause: hereditary, acquired, infectious or non‑infectious.
Infectious diseases spread through contaminated air, water, food or vectors such as mosquitoes, flies or animals.
A pathogen is any microorganism (bacteria, virus, parasite) that can cause disease.
Common infectious diseases: tuberculosis, hepatitis, malaria, dengue, cholera, typhoid, dysentery, swine flu, AIDS, rabies, elephantiasis, plague, chickenpox.
Non‑infectious diseases include cancer, diabetes, heart disease, chronic respiratory disease, osteoporosis, etc.
Key symptoms of dengue: acute fever, headache, vomiting, eye‑socket pain, low platelet count leading to internal bleeding.
Symptoms of malaria: fever, chills, headache, body aches, nausea, vomiting, anemia.
Symptoms of HIV/AIDS: weight loss, fever, night sweats, chronic infections, opportunistic infections.
Symptoms of rabies: fever, hydrophobia (fear of water), aggression, confusion, paralysis.
Preventive measures for dengue: eliminate standing water, use mosquito nets, insecticides, community clean‑up.
Preventive measures for malaria: use insecticide‑treated nets, indoor residual spraying, early diagnosis and treatment.
Preventive measures for swine flu: avoid contact with sick pigs, practice hand hygiene, vaccinate if available.
Preventive measures for HIV: safe sex, avoid sharing needles, use condoms, get tested.
Cancer prevention: avoid tobacco, limit alcohol, eat fruits and vegetables, exercise, maintain healthy weight.
Diabetes prevention: balanced diet, regular exercise, avoid excess sugar, maintain healthy weight.
Heart disease prevention: avoid smoking, control blood pressure, manage cholesterol, exercise regularly.
Vaccination protects against many infectious diseases; schedule varies by age and region.
Generic medicines are equivalent to branded drugs but cheaper; they help make treatment affordable.
Lifestyle factors such as sleep, diet, exercise and stress management influence disease risk.
Regular health check‑ups and early detection improve treatment outcomes.
Public health measures: clean water, proper sanitation, waste disposal, vaccination drives, health education.
Community involvement in mosquito control and waste management reduces disease spread.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of infectious disease classification?
quiz.explain: Hereditary diseases are non‑infectious.

quiz.q: What is the main symptom of hydrophobia in rabies?
quiz.explain: Hydrophobia is extreme fear of water.

quiz.q: Which mosquito species spreads dengue?
quiz.explain: Dengue is transmitted by Aedes aegypti.

quiz.q: Which disease is caused by the virus influenza A (H1N1)?
quiz.explain: Swine flu is caused by influenza A (H1N1).

quiz.q: What does a pathogen do?
quiz.explain: A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a non‑infectious disease?
quiz.explain: Cancer is a non‑infectious disease.

quiz.q: Which preventive measure helps stop malaria spread?
quiz.explain: Insecticide‑treated nets prevent mosquito bites.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of diabetes type 2?
quiz.explain: Obesity and lack of exercise are major causes.

quiz.q: Which disease is transmitted by sharing needles?
quiz.explain: Hepatitis B can spread via contaminated needles.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a symptom of dengue?
quiz.explain: Low platelet count can lead to internal bleeding in dengue.

subject: Science
notes: Newton’s first law: an object stays at rest or moves with constant speed unless a net force acts on it.
A force is an interaction that changes the motion of an object; it can be contact (touch) or non‑contact (magnetic, electric, gravitational).
Contact forces act through direct touch: friction, normal force, tension, applied force, muscular force.
Non‑contact forces act at a distance: gravity, magnetism, electrostatic force, air pressure.
A force is a vector: it has magnitude and direction; its SI unit is the Newton (N).
Pressure is the force applied per unit area; it is a scalar quantity.
Formula: Pressure (P) = Force (F) ÷ Area (A). Units: N/m², called Pascal (Pa).
If the area over which a force is applied increases, pressure decreases for the same force; if area decreases, pressure increases.
The weight of an object is the gravitational force acting on it: W = mg (m = mass, g ≈ 9.8 m/s²).
Buoyant force is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object; it equals the weight of the fluid displaced (Archimedes’ principle).
An object floats if buoyant force > weight, sinks if buoyant force < weight, and stays at a fixed depth if they are equal.
Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air column above a unit area; at sea level it is about 101.3 kPa (1 atm).
Friction opposes motion; kinetic friction acts when objects slide, static friction when they are at rest.
Inertia is the tendency of an object to keep its state of motion; it is the property that resists changes in speed or direction.
Examples of contact forces: pushing a box, pulling a rope, friction between shoes and ground.
Examples of non‑contact forces: gravity pulling a falling apple, magnet pulling a nail, electrostatic attraction between a comb and hair.
Pressure in a fluid is the same in all directions at a point; this isotropy is why a submerged object feels equal pressure from all sides.
The pressure exerted by a fluid on a surface depends on the depth of the fluid; deeper points have higher pressure.
When a solid is placed in water, the water exerts a pressure that can be larger or smaller than the solid’s weight, determining whether it floats or sinks.
The pressure of a gas or liquid is independent of the shape of the container; it depends only on the amount of fluid and its density.
The SI unit of pressure is the Pascal, 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
A larger contact area reduces pressure for a given force, which is why camel feet spread over a wide area to avoid sinking into sand.
When a vehicle has many wheels, each wheel carries less load, reducing the pressure on the road and preventing damage.
The force of gravity is always a non‑contact force acting between masses.
The normal force is the reaction force exerted by a surface to support an object; it acts perpendicular to the surface.

quiz.q: Which law states that an object at rest stays at rest unless acted upon by a force?
quiz.explain: Newton’s First Law, also called the law of inertia.

quiz.q: A force that acts through contact between two bodies is called?
quiz.explain: Contact forces act through physical contact.

quiz.q: If two equal forces act on a body in opposite directions, the net force is
options: Equal to one of the forces
Equal to the sum of the forces
quiz.explain: They cancel each other, giving zero net force.

quiz.q: Pressure is defined as the force applied per unit
quiz.explain: Pressure = Force ÷ Area.

quiz.q: The SI unit of pressure is
quiz.explain: 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

quiz.q: When a liquid is deeper, the pressure at the bottom is
quiz.explain: Pressure increases with depth.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a non‑contact force?
quiz.explain: Magnetic force acts without contact.

quiz.q: A force that acts opposite to the direction of motion is called
quiz.explain: Friction opposes motion.

quiz.q: The atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately
quiz.explain: 1 atm ≈ 101.3 kPa.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about buoyancy?
options: It depends on the shape of the object
It depends on the volume of displaced fluid
It depends on the color of the object
It depends on the temperature of the fluid
quiz.explain: Buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid, which depends on volume.

subject: Science
notes: - An atom contains protons (positive) and electrons (negative).
- In a neutral object, equal numbers of protons and electrons cancel charge.
- Static charge: charge that does not move. Moving charge: electrons moving through a conductor.
- Current is the flow of electrons in a conductor.
- Electric current is measured in amperes (A). 1 A = 1 coulomb per second.
- Potential difference (voltage) is the electric ‘height’ that drives electrons from one point to another.
- The unit of potential difference is the volt (V).
- A dry cell supplies a constant voltage (e.g., 1.5 V).
- In a dry cell, zinc reacts with electrolyte to produce electrons at the negative terminal.
- A lead‑acid cell (battery) gives about 2 V and can be recharged.
- Ni‑Cd cells give about 1.2 V and are rechargeable.
- Connecting cells in series adds their voltages; in parallel the voltage stays the same but capacity increases.
- A simple electric circuit consists of a power source, a load (e.g., bulb) and connecting wires.
- When a current flows through a wire, it creates a magnetic field around the wire.
- An electromagnet is a coil of wire that becomes magnetic when current passes through it.
- In an electric bell, the coil attracts a metal strip, causing a striker to hit a gong and produce sound.
- The current stops when the contact is broken, the magnetism disappears, and the strip returns to the contact, restarting the cycle.

quiz.q: What is the unit of electric current?
quiz.explain: Electric current is measured in amperes (A).

quiz.q: Which particle carries negative charge in an atom?
quiz.explain: Electrons are negatively charged particles in an atom.

quiz.q: A dry cell typically contains which electrolyte?
quiz.explain: Dry cells use a wet pulp of zinc chloride and ammonium chloride as electrolyte.

quiz.q: In a simple electric circuit, when the plug key is opened, what happens to the current?
quiz.explain: Opening the plug key breaks the circuit, stopping the current.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a magnetic effect of electric current?
options: Creation of a magnetic field around a wire
quiz.explain: Electric current flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field around it.

quiz.q: What is the potential difference between the terminals of a typical lead‑acid cell?
quiz.explain: A lead‑acid cell provides about 2 volts between its terminals.

quiz.q: When two cells are connected in series, what happens to the total potential difference?
options: It is the average of the two
It is the sum of the two
It is the product of the two
quiz.explain: Series connection adds the potentials of each cell.

quiz.q: Which device uses an electromagnet to produce sound?
quiz.explain: An electric bell uses an electromagnet to strike a gong.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of electric cell mentioned?
quiz.explain: Lithium‑sulfur cells are not mentioned in the chapter.

quiz.q: What is the main reason a dry cell can be used in any orientation?
options: It is sealed and contains no liquid
quiz.explain: Dry cells are sealed and can be used in any orientation.

subject: Science
notes: Matter is made of atoms, and atoms are the smallest units that keep an element’s identity.
An atom is indivisible and indestructible (Dalton’s view).
Atoms of the same element are identical; different elements have different atoms.
The smallest particle of a compound is a molecule; of an element it is an atom.
Atoms contain a nucleus (protons + neutrons) and electrons orbiting it.
Protons carry +1 charge, neutrons are neutral, electrons carry –1 charge.
Atomic number (Z) = number of protons; mass number (A) = protons + neutrons.
Electrons are arranged in shells (K, L, M, N…) with capacities 2n² (n=1,2,3…).
Valence electrons are those in the outermost shell; they determine chemical bonding.
Valency = number of bonds an atom can form; for most elements it equals the number of valence electrons if ≤4, otherwise 8‑x where x is valence electrons.
Rutherford’s gold‑foil experiment showed most α‑particles pass through, proving atoms have a small, dense nucleus.
Bohr’s model added quantised electron orbits to explain atomic stability and spectral lines.
Isotopes have same Z but different A (different neutron numbers).
Heavy water (D₂O) contains deuterium (²H) instead of normal hydrogen.
In a nuclear reactor, slow neutrons are moderated (e.g., by heavy water) to sustain fission of U‑235.

quiz.q: Which particle carries a positive charge in an atom?
quiz.explain: Protons are positively charged

quiz.q: What does the atomic number of an element represent?
quiz.explain: Atomic number equals the number of protons

quiz.q: In Bohr’s model, electrons occupy stable orbits. What happens when an electron jumps from a higher to a lower orbit?
quiz.explain: Energy is released as a photon

quiz.q: Which experiment proved that atoms have a small, dense nucleus?
quiz.explain: Rutherford scattered α‑particles and observed deflections

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of electrons in the K‑shell?
quiz.explain: Capacity = 2n², n=1 → 2

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a subatomic particle?
quiz.explain: Photon is a particle of light, not subatomic

quiz.q: If an element has 6 valence electrons, what is its valency?
quiz.explain: Valency equals number of valence electrons when ≤4; here 6 >4, so valency = 8‑6 = 2

quiz.q: Which isotope of hydrogen is used in heavy water?
quiz.explain: ²H (deuterium) is the heavy isotope

quiz.q: What is the primary role of a moderator in a nuclear reactor?
quiz.explain: Moderator slows neutrons to sustain fission

quiz.q: What is the mass of an electron relative to a proton?
quiz.explain: Electron mass ≈ 1/1800 of a proton

subject: Science
notes: States of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
Solid has definite shape and volume, particles are close and vibrate in fixed positions.
Liquid has definite volume but takes shape of container, particles are close but can move past each other.
Gas has no definite shape or volume, particles are far apart and move freely.
Intermolecular forces are attractive forces between particles; stronger forces give more rigidity.
In solids the forces are strong, in liquids moderate, in gases weak.
Definite shape and volume → solid; definite volume only → liquid; neither → gas.
Density is mass per unit volume; solids usually have higher density than liquids and gases.
Compressibility is the ability to reduce volume under pressure; solids are hardly compressible, gases are highly compressible.
Molecular formula shows the number of atoms of each element in a molecule.
Valency is the number of chemical bonds an atom can form; hydrogen has valency 1, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3, carbon 4.

Element is a pure substance made of one type of atom; compound is made of two or more different atoms bonded together; mixture is a combination of two or more substances that are not chemically bonded.
Mixtures can be homogeneous (uniform composition, e.g. salt solution) or heterogeneous (different phases, e.g. sand in water).
Colloids are heterogeneous mixtures with particle size between 1 µm and 100 µm, e.g. milk, fog.
In a chemical reaction new substances are formed; the products have properties different from the reactants.
When a solid is heated, it may melt (solid→liquid) or evaporate (solid→gas).
When a liquid is heated, it may boil (liquid→gas).
When a gas is cooled, it may condense (gas→liquid) or freeze (gas→solid).
The law of conservation of mass states that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
In a mixture, the components retain their individual properties; in a compound, the properties are new.
The ratio of elements in a compound is fixed and expressed by its molecular formula.
The strength of intermolecular forces determines the state of matter at a given temperature.
The boiling point of a liquid increases with stronger intermolecular forces.
The melting point of a solid increases with stronger intermolecular forces.
The density of a substance is related to the mass and volume of its particles.

quiz.q: What is the state of matter that has a definite shape and volume?
quiz.explain: Solids have both definite shape and volume.

quiz.q: Which of the following particles move freely and occupy all available space?
quiz.explain: Gases have freely moving particles and fill the container.

quiz.q: Which type of matter is made of atoms of the same element?
quiz.explain: An element consists of identical atoms.

quiz.q: Water is a _______ because it is formed by chemical combination of hydrogen and oxygen.
quiz.explain: Water is a compound.

quiz.q: Milk is an example of a _______ because its components are not chemically bonded.
quiz.explain: Milk is a mixture of several substances.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of liquids?
quiz.explain: Liquids have fluidity and definite volume.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of a homogeneous mixture?
quiz.explain: Milk is a homogeneous mixture (solution).

quiz.q: Which force keeps particles together in a solid?
quiz.explain: Strong intermolecular forces hold solids together.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a complex compound?
quiz.explain: Chlorophyll contains a metal (magnesium) in its structure.

quiz.q: Which state of matter has neither definite shape nor definite volume?
quiz.explain: Gases have no definite shape or volume.

subject: Science
notes: Metals, non‑metals and metalloids are the three broad groups of elements.
Metals are usually solid at room temperature, have a shiny lustre, are hard, ductile and malleable, conduct heat and electricity, and have high melting and boiling points.
Non‑metals are solid, liquid or gas at room temperature, are dull, brittle, poor conductors of heat and electricity, and have low melting and boiling points.
Metalloids have properties intermediate between metals and non‑metals.
Ductility – the ability of a metal to be drawn into a wire; malleability – the ability to be hammered into a sheet.
Lustre – light reflects from a polished metal surface, giving it a shine.
Density – most metals are denser than water; many non‑metals are lighter than water.
Sonority – metals produce a ringing sound when struck.
Noble metals (gold, silver, platinum, palladium, rhodium) are resistant to corrosion and oxidation.
Corrosion – reaction of a metal with oxygen, water or other chemicals forming oxides or other compounds.
Alloys – homogeneous mixtures of two or more metals or a metal with a non‑metal; e.g., stainless steel, bronze, brass.
Oxidation of iron produces rust (Fe₂O₃·nH₂O).
Graphite (an allotrope of carbon) is a good conductor of electricity among non‑metals.
Some non‑metals (e.g., chlorine, iodine) are liquids at room temperature; hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen are gases.
Metals form positive ions (cations) by losing electrons; non‑metals form negative ions (anions) by gaining electrons.
When a metal reacts with a dilute acid it usually forms a salt and releases hydrogen gas.
When a metal reacts with water, only alkali metals (Na, K) react vigorously; others may need steam.
When a metal reacts with oxygen it forms an oxide; metal oxides are usually basic, non‑metal oxides are usually acidic.
The density of a metal can be calculated as mass per unit volume (g/cc).
The melting point of a metal is the temperature at which it changes from solid to liquid; the boiling point is when it changes from liquid to gas.
The colour of a metal can change due to oxidation (e.g., copper turns green due to copper carbonate).
The term ‘noble’ refers to metals that do not corrode easily under normal conditions.
The best conductors of heat are silver, copper and aluminium; the best conductors of electricity are copper, aluminium, silver and gold.
The best conductors of electricity are metals except lead, which is a poor conductor of both heat and electricity.
The best conductors of heat are metals except mercury and gallium, which are liquid at room temperature.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a property of metals?
quiz.explain: Metals are ductile, malleable and dense, but they are not brittle.

quiz.q: Which metal is a noble metal and is used in jewelry?
quiz.explain: Gold is a noble metal and widely used in ornaments.

quiz.q: Which non‑metal is a liquid at room temperature?
quiz.explain: Chlorine is a liquid gas at room temperature.

quiz.q: What happens when a metal reacts with a dilute acid?
options: Forms a salt and releases hydrogen gas
Forms a salt and releases oxygen gas
Forms a salt and releases nitrogen gas
Forms a salt and releases carbon dioxide
quiz.explain: Dilute acids produce metal salts and hydrogen gas.

quiz.q: Which metal is known for its excellent electrical conductivity?
quiz.explain: Copper is one of the best conductors of electricity.

quiz.q: Which property describes a metal’s ability to be hammered into a sheet?
quiz.explain: Malleability is the ability to be hammered into a sheet.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of non‑metals?
quiz.explain: Non‑metals are generally brittle.

quiz.q: What is the term for a mixture of two or more metals?
quiz.explain: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of metals.

quiz.q: Which metal is most resistant to corrosion and is called a noble metal?
quiz.explain: Silver is a noble metal that resists corrosion.

quiz.q: Which metal is used to make electrical wires due to its high conductivity?
quiz.explain: Copper is the best conductor of electricity for wires.

subject: Science
notes: Pollution is the contamination of the environment by harmful substances that damage living organisms and ecosystems.
Air pollution is caused by burning fuels, industrial emissions, vehicle exhaust, and natural events like volcanic eruptions.
Key air pollutants: sulphur dioxide (SO₂), nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), carbon monoxide (CO), particulate matter (PM), dust, and methane (CH₄).
Ozone layer protects life from UV‑B rays; its depletion increases skin cancer and eye irritation.
Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, CFCs) trap heat and cause global warming and climate change.
Acid rain forms when SO₂ and NOₓ mix with rainwater, producing sulphuric and nitric acids, damaging soil, water bodies and structures.
Water pollution comes from biological (bacteria, algae), inorganic (heavy metals, salts) and organic (pesticides, detergents) pollutants.
Soil pollution reduces fertility, alters pH, and introduces toxic metals that enter the food chain.
Preventive measures: use filters in factories, proper waste disposal, ban on CFCs, clean water treatment, and public awareness.
Air Quality Index (AQI) tells how clean or polluted the air is in a city.
Industrial accidents (e.g., Bhopal gas leak) show the severe health impact of toxic gas releases.
Human activities like burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and improper waste disposal are main pollution sources.
Natural causes of pollution include volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, dust storms, and forest fires.
Vehicles with two‑stroke engines emit more pollutants than four‑stroke engines because of incomplete combustion.
Water bodies become polluted when sewage, industrial effluents, and agricultural runoff enter them.
Air, water, and soil pollution are interrelated; waste dumped in one medium can contaminate the others.
Legislation such as the Water Pollution Prevention Act (1974), Air Pollution Prevention Act (1981), and Environmental Protection Act (1986) regulate pollution control.
Public bodies like the Central Pollution Control Board supervise compliance with pollution laws.
Preventive actions: use clean energy, recycle waste, plant trees, and maintain proper sanitation.
Education and community participation are essential for effective pollution control.

subject: Science
notes: Disaster is a sudden event causing loss of life, property and environment.
Natural disasters: earthquakes, floods, landslides, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions, cyclones, droughts, forest fires.
Man‑made disasters: industrial accidents, chemical spills, nuclear incidents, fires, dam failures.
Earthquake: sudden vibration of earth’s surface caused by release of stress in rocks.
Epicentre: point on surface directly above focus of earthquake.
Seismograph/Seismometer records seismic waves; intensity measured on Richter scale.
Richter scale: logarithmic scale; each unit increase = 10× amplitude, 31.6× energy.
Effects of earthquakes: loss of life, economic damage, ecosystem destruction, river course changes, tsunami if ocean floor disturbed.
Precautions during earthquake: stay indoors, drop, cover, hold; avoid windows, tall objects, elevators.
Earthquake‑resistant buildings: designed per IS 1893, IS 456, IS 13920; use ductile detailing, base isolation, reinforced concrete.
Fire: rapid oxidation of material; can be natural or man‑made.
Fire classes: A (solid), B (liquid), C (gas), D (combustible metal), E (electrical).
Extinguishing methods: water (Class A), foam/spray (Class B), CO₂ (Class C), dry powder (Class D), CO₂ or dry chemical (Class E).
Landslide: rapid movement of rock/soil down slope due to water, earthquakes, deforestation, construction.
Causes of landslides: heavy rains, earthquakes, deforestation, slope cutting, dam failure.
Disaster relief planning: create school disaster plan, conduct mock drills, maintain emergency supplies, map safe zones.
Key terms: epicentre, focus, Richter scale, seismic wave, tsunami, base isolation, ductile detailing, CO₂ extinguisher, foam extinguisher, landslide.
Safety measures: switch off gas and electricity during fire, call fire brigade, use non‑conductive extinguishers for electrical fires.
Emergency map: shows buildings, exits, safe zones, nearest roads.
Mock drill: schedule monthly, record participants, note shortcomings.

प्लांटा: बहुपेशीय, स्वयंपोषी, प्रकाशसंश्लेषण, पेशीभित्तिका सेलुलोजची.
अॅनिमालिया: बहुपेशीय, परपोषी, पेशीभित्तिका नसते, पोषण भक्षक किंवा विघटक.

जीवाणूंचे प्रजनन बहुधा द्विखंडीभवनाने होते, 20 मिनिटांत दुप्पट होऊ शकतात.

कवकांची पेशीभित्तिका कायटीनची बनलेली असते, बहुतेक मृतोपजीवी असतात.
शैवाल एकपेशीय किंवा बहुपेशीय असू शकतात, स्वयंपोषी, प्रकाशसंश्लेषण करतात.
वर्गीकरणात पाच प्रमुख निकष: पेशीची जटिलता, पेशीची संख्या, पोषण प्रकार, जीवनपद्धती, वंशपरंपरागत संबंध.
सजीवांचे वर्गीकरण केल्याने त्यांच्या वैशिष्ट्यांची ओळख पटते आणि रोगकारकांची ओळख सोपी होते.
सजीवांचे वर्गीकरण प्रयोगशाळेत सूक्ष्मदर्शकाने निरीक्षण करून केले जाते.
वर्गीकरण पद्धतींचे फायदे: स्पष्टता, तुलना, संशोधन सुलभता.
वर्गीकरण पद्धतींचे तोटे: काही सजीवांचे वर्गीकरण अस्पष्ट.
सजीवांचे वर्गीकरण करताना गुणधर्मांची तुलना करणे आवश्यक.
वर्गीकरणामुळे सूक्ष्मजीवांच्या रोगकारकांची ओळख आणि उपचार सोपे होतात.
वर्गीकरणात पाच सृष्टींचे समावेश: मोनेरा, प्रोटिस्टा, फंगी, प्लांटा, अॅनिमालिया.
वर्गीकरणात पाच प्रमुख निकषांचा वापर केला जातो.
वर्गीकरण पद्धतींचे फायदे: स्पष्टता, तुलना, संशोधन सुलभता.

notes: पेशी हे सजीवांचे रचनात्मक व कार्यात्मक एकक आहे.
वनस्पती पेशीला पेशीभित्तिका आणि पेशीपटल दोन्ही असतात, प्राणी पेशीला फक्त पेशीपटल असते.
पेशीभित्तिका सेल्युलोज व पेक्टीनपासून बनलेली असते, ज्यामुळे पेशीला आधार व रक्षण मिळते.
पेशीपटल हे पातळ, लवचिक आवरण असून निवडक्षम (selective) पारगम्य असते.
पेशीपटलातून पाणी व वायूंचा प्रवास विसरण व परासरण या प्रक्रियेद्वारे होतो.
विसरण: लहान रेणूंचा यादृच्छिक हालचाल; परासरण: पाण्याचा प्रवास जास्त पाण्याच्या भागातून कमी पाण्याच्या भागाकडे.
अवसरासारी द्रावणात पेशीतील पाण्यापेक्षा बाहेरील पाण्याचे प्रमाण जास्त असते, त्यामुळे पाणी पेशीत शिरते.
अतिपरासारी द्रावणात पेशीतील पाण्यापेक्षा बाहेरील पाण्याचे प्रमाण कमी असते, त्यामुळे पाणी पेशीतून बाहेर पडते (रससंकोच).
पेशीद्रव्य हे पेशीतील तरल पदार्थ असून त्यात प्रथिने, एंझाईम व इतर अंगके असतात.
केंद्रकात दुहेरी आवरण व केंद्रकी असते, ज्यात गुणसूत्रे व जनुके असतात.
केंद्रक पेशीच्या चयापचय व विभाजनावर नियंत्रण ठेवते.
आंतर्द्रव्यजालिका (ER) प्रथिनांचे संश्लेषण व परिवहन करते; खडबडीत ER वर रायबोझोम्स असतात.
गॉल्गी संकुल प्रथिनांचे परिष्करण व पॅकेजिंग करते, नंतर बाहेर पाठवते.
लयकारिका (लायसोजोम) पेशीतील टाकाऊ पदार्थांचे पचन करते व रोगप्रतिकारात मदत करते.
रिक्तिका पाण्याचे व इतर पदार्थांचे साठवण करते; वनस्पती रिक्तिकेने पेशीला ताठरता देते.

पेशीतील पाण्याचे प्रमाण व दाब परासरणाने नियंत्रित होते.

notes: मानवी शरीरात इंद्रिय संस्था म्हणजे विविध इंद्रिये एकत्र काम करून जीवनक्रिया पार पाडणारे समूह.

श्वसनाची तीन टप्पे – बाह्य श्वसन (हवा नाकातून फुफ्फुसात घेणे व बाहेर सोडणे), अंतः श्वसन (पेशी व रक्तामधील वायूंची देवाणघेवाण), पेशी श्वसन (ऑक्सिजन व ग्लुकोजचे ज्वलन करून ऊर्जा निर्मिती).
पेशी श्वसनाचे समीकरण: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + ऊर्जा (उष्णता).
फुफ्फुसातील वायूकोश (अल्विओलाय) हे वायूंची देवाणघेवाण करणारे सूक्ष्म पोकळ्या आहेत.
रक्ताभिसरणात हृदय, रक्तवाहिन्या (धमनी, शिरा) व केशिका यांचा समावेश होतो.
धमनींची भित्ती जाड असते व झडपा नसतात; शिरांची भित्ती पातळ असते व झडपा असतात.
केशिका पातळ भित्ती व केशवाहिन्यांचे जाळे असते, ज्याद्वारे वायू व पोषक तत्त्वांची देवाणघेवाण होते.
रक्ताचे प्रमुख घटक – प्लाझ्मा (सुमारे 90-92%), लाल रक्तपेशी (RBC), पांढऱ्या रक्तपेशी (WBC), प्लेटलेट्स.
रक्ताचे कार्य – वायूंचे परिवहन, पोषणतत्त्वांचे वितरण, टाकाऊ पदार्थांचे बहन, शरीररक्षण, संप्रेरक व बारीक पदार्थांचे परिवहन, तापमान नियमन, क्षारांचा समतोल राखणे.
रक्तगट – A, B, AB, O आणि Rh घटकांनुसार 8 प्रकार. रक्तदान करताना रक्तगट जुळणे आवश्यक.
रक्तदाब – सिस्टॉलिक (हृदय आकुंचन) व डायस्टॉलिक (हृदय प्रसरण) दाब. सामान्य रक्तदाब 120/80 मिमीHg.
हृदयाचे स्पंदन – प्रत्येक आकुंचन व शिथिलीकरणाने एक ठोका. प्रति मिनिट 60-100 ठोके सामान्य.
श्वसनक्रिया – नाक, घसा, श्वासनलिका, फुफ्फुस, श्वसनपटल या भागांची रचना व कार्य.
रक्ताभिसरणाचा पंप – हृदयाचे स्नायू अनैच्छिक असून तालबद्ध आकुंचन करतात.
श्वसनपटल (डायाफ्राम) हे बरगड्यांखालील स्नायू असून श्वसनाच्या वेळी वर-खाली हालचाल करते.
श्वसनाच्या वेळी फुफ्फुसांवरील दाब कमी होऊन हवा आत व बाहेर जाते.
रक्ताभिसरणात रक्तवाहिन्यांमधून रक्त सतत फिरते, ज्यामुळे शरीरातील सर्व अवयवांना पोषण व ऑक्सिजन मिळतो.
रक्तातील लाल रक्तपेशीतील हिमोग्लोबीन ऑक्सिजन बंधून वाहून नेतो.
पांढऱ्या रक्तपेशी रोगप्रतिकारक शक्तीचे कार्य करतात.
रक्तदाब मोजण्यासाठी स्पिग्मोमॅनोमीटर वापरले जाते.
रक्तदानासाठी व्यक्तीचे आरोग्य चांगले असणे, रक्तगट जुळणे, आणि रक्ताचे प्रमाण (350 ml) हे निकष आहेत.

options: सर्व इंद्रिये एकत्र काम करणारा समूह
