subject: History & Civics
notes: Historical sources are divided into written, oral, material, and audio-visual types.
Written sources include books, letters, official records, and newspapers.
Oral sources consist of folk songs, powadas, inspirational speeches, and interviews.
Material sources are physical objects like tools, coins, pottery, and monuments.
Audio-visual sources include photographs, films, recordings, and videos.
Photographs provide visual details about people, events, places, and structures.
Films help us see historical events as they happened, such as the Dandi Yatra or Quit India Movement.
Recordings preserve speeches and songs of leaders like Mahatma Gandhi and Subhash Chandra Bose.
Powadas are Marathi ballads that narrate heroic deeds and inspire during freedom struggles.
Inspirational songs motivated people during the freedom movement and are preserved in oral tradition.
Newspapers during British rule spread awareness and supported social reform movements.
Archives preserve written sources, but author bias must be checked for authenticity.
Photographs are considered more reliable than paintings for showing real physical features.
Modern technology like photography, recording, and filmmaking greatly enriched historical sources.
It is important to preserve historical sources so future generations can learn from them.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of an audio-visual source of history?
quiz.explain: Films are audio-visual sources as they combine visual images and sound to record events.

quiz.q: Which source type includes folk songs and inspirational speeches?
quiz.explain: Oral sources consist of spoken or sung traditions like powadas, songs, and interviews.

quiz.q: What does a photograph of a historical structure mainly help us understand?
quiz.explain: Photographs give visual details about the appearance, structure, and design of objects or buildings.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a written source?
quiz.explain: Photographs are visual (audio-visual) sources, not written, as they do not contain text.

quiz.q: Which museum in Pune is related to Mahatma Gandhi’s history?
quiz.explain: Aga Khan Palace in Pune is where Gandhi was imprisoned and now houses a memorial to him.

quiz.q: What technological development in the 20th century allowed recording of leaders’ speeches?
quiz.explain: The invention of audio recording enabled preservation of speeches and songs as historical sources.

quiz.q: Why are photographs considered more reliable than medieval paintings for historical study?
options: They capture real physical features accurately
quiz.explain: Photographs show actual appearance, while paintings may reflect artist’s imagination or bias.

quiz.q: Which of these is a source of modern Indian history due to technological advancement?
quiz.explain: Films are a 20th-century technological development and serve as important audio-visual sources.

quiz.q: What kind of source is a Powada?
quiz.explain: Powada is a traditional Marathi ballad sung or recited, making it an oral source of history.

quiz.q: During the British period, how did newspapers contribute to society?
options: By spreading awareness and supporting reform
quiz.explain: Newspapers spread ideas of freedom and social reform, helping awaken public consciousness.

subject: History & Civics
notes: - Equality means giving everyone the same rights and opportunities regardless of caste, class, gender or religion.
- In India, the struggle for equality began in the 19th and 20th centuries with movements by peasants, workers, women and Dalits.
- Peasant movements fought against feudal landlords, money lenders and the forced cultivation of indigo and cotton.
- Workers’ unions such as the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) were formed in 1920 to protect workers’ rights and wages.
- Women’s reform movements (e.g., Satyashodhak Samaj, Arya Mahila Samaj) fought for education, voting rights and against social discrimination.
- Dalit movements led by leaders like Gopal Baba Walangkar, Shivram Janba Kamble and Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar sought to abolish untouchability and caste discrimination.
- The Congress Socialist Party (1934) and the Communist Party (1925) also contributed to the fight for social justice.
- Key laws: The Indian Constitution (1949) guarantees equality; the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (1989) protects Dalits.
- Important slogans: “Educate, Organise, Agitate” (Gandhi), “Be Educated, Be Organised, Be Agitated” (Satyashodhak Samaj).
- The Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929) was a major crackdown on communist activists.
- The Mahad Satyagraha (1927) led by Dr. Ambedkar opened a public water tank for Dalits.
- The Red Cross Society was founded by Rakhmabai Save to help women and children.
- The first Indian women doctors were Dr. Anandibai Joshi (1886) and Dr. Rakhmabai Save (1925).
- The “Kisan Sabha” (1918) was a farmers’ union that demanded land reforms.
- The “Bombay Mill Hands Association” (1890) was an early workers’ union in Mumbai.
- The “All India Women’s Conference” (1927) promoted women’s rights and education.
- The “All India Scheduled Castes Federation” (1934) fought for Dalit rights.
- The “Bahishkrut Bharat” newspaper was started by Ambedkar to spread his ideas.
- The “Satyagraha” movement used non‑violent protest to challenge social injustices.
- The “Balutedari System” was abolished in 1918 in Kolhapur to free Dalits from bonded labour.
- The “Khandesh” region saw peasant revolts in 1938 due to heavy rains and crop destruction.
- The “Kisan Sabha” and “AITUC” were instrumental in shaping modern Indian labour law.
- The “Red Cross Society” at Rajkot was opened by Sane Guruji to help the poor.
- The “All India Trade Union Congress” was led by Lala Lajpat Rai and Narayan Meghaji Lokhande in its early years.
- The “Satyashodhak Samaj” was founded by Jyotirao Phle and Mahatma Phule to fight untouchability.

quiz.q: Which movement fought against forced cultivation of indigo in Bengal?
quiz.explain: The Indigo Rebellion was a peasant uprising against indigo cultivation.

quiz.q: Who founded the All India Trade Union Congress in 1920?
quiz.explain: Narayan Meghaji Lokhande was the first president of AITUC.

quiz.q: The Mahad Satyagraha was led by which leader?
quiz.explain: Ambedkar organized the Mahad Satyagraha to open a public water tank.

quiz.q: Which act abolished the Balutedari System in Kolhapur?
quiz.explain: The Balutedari System Abolition Act of 1918 freed Dalits from bonded labour.

quiz.q: The Red Cross Society in Rajkot was founded by whom?
quiz.explain: Rakhmabai Save established the Red Cross Society in Rajkot.

quiz.q: Which newspaper was started by Dr. Ambedkar to spread his ideas?
quiz.explain: Ambedkar started the newspaper Muknayak.

quiz.q: The Congress Socialist Party was formed in which year?
quiz.explain: It was formed in 1934 as a socialist wing of the Congress.

quiz.q: The Satyashodhak Samaj was founded by which reformer?
quiz.explain: Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj to fight untouchability.

quiz.q: The Meerut Conspiracy Case was a crackdown on which group?
quiz.explain: It targeted communist activists accused of conspiracy.

quiz.q: Which slogan was used by the Satyashodhak Samaj?
options: Be Educated, Be Organised, Be Agitated
quiz.explain: The Satyashodhak Samaj used that slogan.

subject: History & Civics
notes: India gained independence on 15 August 1947 after years of struggle by the Indian National Congress and other groups.
The British government, after World‑II, realised it could not keep India under its rule and started planning for independence.
The Cabinet Mission of 1946 was a British plan to give India a constitution and decide on partition, but it was not accepted by all parties.
The Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, demanded a separate Muslim state – Pakistan – and rejected the Cabinet Mission plan.
The Wavell Plan (1945) suggested a federal structure for India but was rejected by the Muslim League and did not work.
Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) was called by the Muslim League to demand Pakistan; it led to widespread riots.
The Interim Government was formed in 1946 with leaders from both Congress and Muslim League but could not function smoothly.
Lord Mountbatten was appointed as the last Viceroy and helped draft the Indian Independence Act of 1947.
The Indian Independence Act, passed on 18 August 1947, ended British rule and created two independent dominions – India and Pakistan.
The Indian flag was raised at midnight on 15 August 1947, replacing the Union Jack.
The Partition caused massive displacement and communal violence across the sub‑continent.
Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948, shortly after independence.
The Constitution of India was drafted by the Constituent Assembly, which met in Delhi from 1946 to 1950.
The princely states were given the option to join India or Pakistan or remain independent, but most joined India.
India’s independence marked the end of 150 years of British colonial rule in the sub‑continent.

quiz.q: Which plan was proposed by the British in 1946 to give India a constitution and decide on partition?
quiz.explain: The Cabinet Mission was a 1946 British plan to draft a constitution and decide on partition.

quiz.q: What was the main demand of the Muslim League in 1946?
options: A united India with special Muslim rights
A separate Muslim state called Pakistan
quiz.explain: The Muslim League demanded a separate Muslim state, which became Pakistan.

quiz.q: Who was the last Viceroy of India?
quiz.explain: Lord Mountbatten was appointed as the last Viceroy and helped draft the Independence Act.

quiz.q: When was Direct Action Day declared by the Muslim League?
quiz.explain: Direct Action Day was called on 16 August 1946 to demand Pakistan.

quiz.q: Which act ended British rule in India on 15 August 1947?
quiz.explain: The Indian Independence Act of 1947 ended British rule.

quiz.q: What was the main reason the Interim Government could not function smoothly?
quiz.explain: All of the above factors hindered the Interim Government.

quiz.q: Which leader was assassinated on 30 January 1948?
quiz.explain: Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948.

quiz.q: What did the Indian Independence Act allow princely states to do?
quiz.explain: The Act gave princely states the choice to join India or Pakistan.

quiz.q: Which plan suggested a federal structure for India but was rejected by the Muslim League?
quiz.explain: The Wavell Plan proposed a federal structure but was rejected.

quiz.q: Who was the leader of the Indian National Congress during independence?
quiz.explain: Jawaharlal Nehru became the first Prime Minister of independent India.

subject: History & Civics
notes: India gained independence on 15 August 1947 but many princely states were still independent.
The Indian government invited all princely states to join either India or Pakistan.
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel negotiated with the rulers and secured the accession of most states.
Junagadh, a princely state in Saurashtra, initially wanted to join Pakistan but after a referendum it merged with India in 1948.
Hyderabad was the largest princely state; its ruler, the Nizam, wanted independence. Operation Polo (1948) integrated Hyderabad into India.
Kashmir was ruled by Maharaja Hari Singh. Facing invasion by tribal militias from Pakistan, he signed the Instrument of Accession to India in 1947.
The Portuguese controlled Goa, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, and Daman & Diu. In 1961 India liberated these territories by military action.
The French controlled small enclaves like Chandernagore, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam. They were handed over to India after 1949 plebiscites.
The Marathwada region played a key role in the struggle for Hyderabad’s liberation through the Hyderabad State Congress and Praja Mandals.
The Goa Liberation Movement was led by Dr. T. B. Kunha and the Goa Mukti Samiti, using Satyagraha and armed resistance.
The Instrument of Accession is a legal document by which a princely state joins India, giving the Indian government control over defence, foreign affairs and communications.
The Instrument of Accession was signed by the rulers of Hyderabad, Kashmir, and other princely states.
The integration of princely states was completed by 1948, ending the era of independent princely states in India.
The term ‘Praja Mandal’ means ‘people’s organization’ and was formed to demand political rights in princely states.
The Indian Army’s Operation Polo was a brief but decisive campaign that ended the Nizam’s rule.
The liberation of Goa was celebrated on 19 December 1961, known as Goa Liberation Day.
The integration of French colonies was completed in 1954 after plebiscites.
The integration of Junagadh was decided by a plebiscite held in 1948.
The integration of Hyderabad was achieved through a combination of political persuasion and military action.
The integration of Kashmir was a result of the Maharaja’s decision to accede to India after tribal invasion.
The integration of Dadra & Nagar Haveli was achieved by a small armed force in 1961.
The integration of Goa involved both Satyagraha and a military operation in 1961.
The integration of French colonies involved local plebiscites and negotiations with France.
The integration of princely states was a major achievement of the early Indian republic.
The integration of princely states helped create a unified Indian nation-state.

quiz.q: Which day marks the beginning of independent India?
quiz.explain: India’s independence day is 15 August 1947.

quiz.q: Who was the chief negotiator who secured the accession of most princely states?
quiz.explain: Sardar Patel negotiated with princely rulers.

quiz.q: What was the name of the military operation that integrated Hyderabad into India?
quiz.explain: Operation Polo was the 1948 campaign.

quiz.q: Which princely state was ruled by Maharaja Hari Singh?
quiz.explain: Hari Singh was the Maharaja of Kashmir.

quiz.q: Which document does a princely ruler sign to join India?
quiz.explain: The Instrument of Accession is the legal document.

quiz.q: Which territory was liberated by India in 1961 through a military operation?
quiz.explain: Goa was liberated in 1961.

quiz.q: What was the main strategy used by the Goa Liberation Movement?
quiz.explain: Both Satyagraha and armed resistance were used.

quiz.q: Which French enclave was handed over to India after a 1954 plebiscite?
quiz.explain: Chandernagore was handed over after the plebiscite.

quiz.q: What was the primary reason Junagadh merged with India?
options: It was annexed by the Nizam
quiz.explain: A plebiscite in 1948 led to its merger.

quiz.q: Who led the Hyderabad State Congress during the struggle for Hyderabad’s liberation?
quiz.explain: Swami Ramananda Tirth was a key leader.

subject: History & Civics
notes: Formation of Maharashtra state on linguistic basis after independence.
Demand for Marathi-speaking state grew from early 20th century.
Samyukta Maharashtra Movement aimed to unite all Marathi-speaking regions including Mumbai.
Dar Commission (1948) rejected linguistic states at that time.
JVP Committee (1948-49) accepted linguistic states in principle but delayed implementation.
Nagpur Pact (1953) assured equitable development for Vidarbha and Marathwada.
States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created bilingual Bombay State (Marathi and Gujarati).
Continued agitation led to formation of separate Maharashtra and Gujarat states on 1 May 1960.
Yashwantrao Chavan became the first Chief Minister of Maharashtra.
Hutatma Smarak in Mumbai commemorates 106 martyrs of the movement.
Newspapers like Kesari, Sakal, Navakal and Shahirs played key role in spreading awareness.
Leaders like Senapati Bapat, Acharya Atre, Comrade Dange guided the movement.
Samyukta Maharashtra Samiti coordinated the movement from 1956 onwards.
Mumbai's inclusion in Maharashtra was a major demand and finally achieved in 1960.
Article 371(2) provided special provisions for Vidarbha and Marathwada in Maharashtra.

quiz.q: On which date was the state of Maharashtra officially formed?
quiz.explain: Maharashtra was formed on 1 May 1960 after the Bombay Reorganisation Act.

quiz.q: Which commission was appointed in 1948 to study the formation of linguistic provinces?
quiz.explain: The Dar Commission was appointed on 17 June 1948 under Justice S.K. Dar.

quiz.q: Who was the chairman of the JVP Committee formed in December 1948?
quiz.explain: JVP Committee included Nehru, Patel, and Pattabhi Sitaramayya; named after their initials.

quiz.q: What was the main outcome of the Nagpur Pact of 1953?
options: Assurance of equitable development for Vidarbha and Marathwada
quiz.explain: The Nagpur Pact assured fair financial and developmental provisions for Vidarbha and Marathwada.

quiz.q: Which article was added to the Constitution in 1956 to provide special provisions for certain regions of Maharashtra?

quiz.q: Who became the first Chief Minister of Maharashtra after its formation in 1960?

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the 'Hutatma Smarak' erected in Mumbai?
options: To honour the formation of Gujarat
To commemorate 106 martyrs of the Samyukta Maharashtra Movement
To celebrate the bilingual Bombay State
quiz.explain: Hutatma Smarak near Flora Fountain was built in memory of 106 people who died in police firing during the movement.

quiz.q: Which of the following leaders was NOT associated with the Samyukta Maharashtra Movement?
quiz.explain: Mahatma Gandhi died in 1948 and was not directly involved in the post-independence Maharashtra statehood movement.

subject: History & Civics
notes: Parliamentary system is a form of government where the executive is responsible to the legislature.
India adopted the parliamentary system from England, where it developed historically.
The Indian Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha, and Rajya Sabha.
Lok Sabha members are directly elected by the people; Rajya Sabha members are indirectly elected.
The party with more than half the seats in Lok Sabha forms the government; its leader becomes Prime Minister.
If no party gets a majority, parties may form a coalition government.
The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
A vote of no-confidence can remove the government if it loses the legislature's confidence.
The legislature (Parliament) is supreme and discusses public welfare, laws, and policies.
Opposition parties participate in discussions, suggest improvements, and check government power.
India adopted this system due to familiarity during British rule and discussions in the Constituent Assembly.
The parliamentary system ensures accountability through regular elections and legislative oversight.
Collective responsibility means the entire Council of Ministers is answerable for decisions of any ministry.
The President is the nominal head; real executive power lies with the Prime Minister and Cabinet.
Parliamentary system encourages debate, representation, and responsiveness to public opinion.

quiz.q: Who is the head of the government in India's parliamentary system?
quiz.explain: The Prime Minister is the head of government and leads the Council of Ministers.

quiz.q: Which house of Parliament has members directly elected by the people?
quiz.explain: Lok Sabha members are directly elected; Rajya Sabha members are elected by state legislatures.

quiz.q: What is the term for a government formed when no single party gets a majority?
quiz.explain: When no party has a clear majority, parties join to form a coalition government.

quiz.q: To whom is the Council of Ministers responsible in a parliamentary system?
quiz.explain: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha and must retain its confidence.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of 'collective responsibility' in a parliamentary system?
options: The entire Council is answerable for decisions of any ministry
quiz.explain: Collective responsibility means the whole Council of Ministers stands or falls together.

quiz.q: Which country is considered the origin of the parliamentary system?
quiz.explain: The parliamentary system developed historically in England.

quiz.q: What happens if the Lok Sabha passes a vote of no-confidence against the government?
quiz.explain: A vote of no-confidence means the government has lost the legislature's confidence and must resign.

quiz.q: Who is the nominal head of the Indian state in the parliamentary system?
quiz.explain: The President is the constitutional (nominal) head; real power lies with the Prime Minister.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key feature of the parliamentary system?
options: Executive is part of legislature and responsible to it
quiz.explain: In parliamentary systems, ministers are usually members of legislature and accountable to it.

quiz.q: Why did India adopt the parliamentary system?
options: It was imposed by foreign powers
Due to familiarity during British rule and Constituent Assembly debates
Because it is the only system in the world
quiz.explain: India adopted it due to experience under British rule and extensive discussions in the Constituent Assembly.

subject: History & Civics
notes: India follows a parliamentary system of government where the executive is responsible to the legislature.
The President of India is the nominal head of state, while the Prime Minister is the real head of government.
The Parliament of India consists of the President, Lok Sabha, and Rajya Sabha.
Lok Sabha is the lower house, directly elected by the people, with a term of five years.
Rajya Sabha is the upper house, with members indirectly elected by state legislative assemblies, and is a permanent body.
One-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every two years, ensuring continuity.
Lok Sabha has a maximum strength of 552 members, including up to 20 from Union Territories and 2 nominated Anglo-Indian members.
Rajya Sabha has a total of 250 members: 238 elected from states and UTs, and 12 nominated by the President.
Money Bills can only be introduced in Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha can only delay them by 14 days.
The Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over its meetings and maintains order; the Vice President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
Parliament's main functions include law-making, financial control, overseeing the executive, and amending the Constitution.
A responsible government means the Council of Ministers is accountable to Parliament and can be removed by a vote of no confidence.
Opposition parties play a vital role in scrutinizing government policies and ensuring accountability.
To contest Lok Sabha elections, a person must be an Indian citizen and at least 25 years old.
To contest Rajya Sabha elections, a person must be an Indian citizen and at least 30 years old.

quiz.q: Who is the real head of the government in India's parliamentary system?
quiz.explain: The Prime Minister is the real head of government, while the President is the nominal head.

quiz.q: What is the term of Lok Sabha?
quiz.explain: Lok Sabha has a fixed term of five years unless dissolved earlier.

quiz.q: Which house of Parliament is known as the permanent house?
quiz.explain: Rajya Sabha is a permanent body and is not subject to dissolution.

quiz.q: How many members are nominated by the President to Rajya Sabha?
quiz.explain: The President nominates 12 members to Rajya Sabha from fields like literature, science, arts, and social service.

quiz.q: Which house has the exclusive power to introduce Money Bills?
quiz.explain: Money Bills can only be introduced in Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha cannot initiate them.

quiz.q: What is the minimum age to contest Lok Sabha elections?
quiz.explain: A candidate must be at least 25 years old to contest Lok Sabha elections.

quiz.q: Who is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha?
quiz.explain: The Vice President of India serves as the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of Parliament?
quiz.explain: Conducting elections is the function of the Election Commission, not Parliament.

quiz.q: What does 'responsible government' mean in the parliamentary system?
options: The President is responsible to the people
The Council of Ministers is responsible to Parliament
The judiciary is responsible to the executive
The bureaucracy is responsible to the legislature
quiz.explain: In a responsible government, the Council of Ministers remains in office only as long as it has the confidence of the legislature.

quiz.q: How often are one-third of the members of Rajya Sabha retired?
quiz.explain: One-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every two years to ensure continuity.

subject: History & Civics
notes: The Union Executive includes the President, Prime Minister, and Council of Ministers.
The President is the nominal head of state; the Prime Minister is the executive head.
The President is indirectly elected by an Electoral College of elected MPs and MLAs.
To be eligible for President, one must be an Indian citizen aged 35 or above.
The President's term is five years and can be re-elected.
The President summons, prorogues, addresses, and dissolves Parliament.
No bill becomes law without the President's assent.
The President appoints the Prime Minister, judges, governors, and other key officials.
The President is the Supreme Commander of the defence forces.
The President has judicial powers to grant pardons, reprieves, or reduce punishments.
The President can declare three types of emergencies: National, State, and Financial.
Impeachment is the process to remove the President for violating the Constitution.
The Vice-President acts as President in their absence and is elected by both Houses of Parliament.
The Prime Minister is usually the leader of the majority party in Lok Sabha.
The Prime Minister forms the Council of Ministers and allocates portfolios.
The Prime Minister chairs Cabinet meetings and coordinates government policies.
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
A constitutional amendment limits the Council of Ministers to 15% of Lok Sabha strength.
The Prime Minister aids and advises the President in exercising executive powers.
Parliament controls the executive through debates, question hour, and votes of confidence.

quiz.q: Who is the nominal head of the Indian State?
quiz.explain: The President is the nominal head of state, while the Prime Minister is the real executive head.

quiz.q: How is the President of India elected?
options: By an Electoral College of MPs and MLAs
quiz.explain: The President is indirectly elected by an Electoral College consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies.

quiz.q: What is the minimum age to contest for the President of India?
quiz.explain: A candidate must be an Indian citizen who has completed 35 years of age to be eligible for the Presidency.

quiz.q: Who administers the oath of office to the President of India?
quiz.explain: The Chief Justice of India administers the oath of office to the President.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a power of the President?
options: Removing a judge of the Supreme Court
Being the Supreme Commander of the defence forces
quiz.explain: The President appoints judges but cannot remove them; removal requires impeachment by Parliament.

quiz.q: Who acts as the President in case of vacancy or absence?
quiz.explain: The Vice-President discharges the functions of the President during vacancy or absence.

quiz.q: What is the term of the President of India?
quiz.explain: The President holds office for a term of five years from the date of assuming office.

quiz.q: Which house is known as the permanent house and is not subject to dissolution?
quiz.explain: Rajya Sabha is a permanent body; one-third of its members retire every two years, but it is never dissolved.

quiz.q: Who nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha?
quiz.explain: The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in art, literature, science, and social service.

quiz.q: What is the maximum limit on the number of ministers in the Council of Ministers as per the 91st Amendment?
quiz.explain: The 91st Amendment limits the Council of Ministers to not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the Lok Sabha.

subject: History & Civics
notes: Judiciary is one of the three organs of government, along with legislature and executive.
The judiciary interprets laws and delivers justice to protect citizens' rights.
India has a single, integrated judicial system for the entire country.
The Supreme Court is the apex court, headed by the Chief Justice of India.
High Courts exist in each state; there are currently 24 High Courts in India.
District and lower courts function under the supervision of High Courts.
Judges are appointed by the President and enjoy security of tenure.
Supreme Court judges retire at 65 years; High Court judges at 62 years.
Judges' salaries are paid from the Consolidated Fund of India, not debated in Parliament.
Judicial Review is the power of courts to strike down laws violating the Constitution.
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) allows citizens to approach courts for public welfare issues.
Judicial Activism refers to courts actively promoting justice and equality beyond traditional roles.
Contempt of Court punishes criticism that undermines judicial authority and independence.
Impeachment is the process to remove judges for proven misconduct or incapacity.
The rule of law ensures equality before law for all citizens, regardless of status.

quiz.q: Who appoints the Chief Justice of India and other judges of the Supreme Court?
quiz.explain: The President appoints the Chief Justice and other Supreme Court judges under constitutional provisions.

quiz.q: What is the retirement age for judges of the Supreme Court of India?
quiz.explain: Supreme Court judges retire at the age of 65 years as per constitutional provision.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the High Court?
options: Advising the Governor on district court appointments
quiz.explain: High Courts do not appoint the Prime Minister; that is the President's role based on parliamentary majority.

quiz.q: What does Judicial Review mean in the Indian context?
options: Striking down laws violating the Constitution
quiz.explain: Judicial Review is the power of judiciary to declare laws or executive actions unconstitutional and void.

quiz.q: Which court is known as the apex court in India?
quiz.explain: The Supreme Court is the highest judicial authority in India, below which are High Courts and subordinate courts.

quiz.q: How many High Courts are currently there in India?
quiz.explain: There are 24 High Courts in India, one in each state or shared among states.

quiz.q: What is Public Interest Litigation (PIL)?
options: A case filed by the government
A case filed by a lawyer for profit
A case filed by citizens for public welfare
A case about criminal punishment only
quiz.explain: PIL allows individuals or organizations to approach courts on behalf of the public for issues affecting society at large.

quiz.q: From which fund are the salaries of judges in India paid?
quiz.explain: Judges' salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India to ensure financial independence from Parliament.

quiz.q: What is the term of the President of India?
quiz.explain: The President of India is elected for a term of five years from the date of assuming office.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a reason for maintaining judicial independence?
options: To allow Parliament to override court decisions
To enable judges to give justice without fear or favor
To let the executive control court judgments
To reduce the number of courts in the country
quiz.explain: Judicial independence ensures judges can perform their duties impartially without pressure from legislature or executive.

subject: History & Civics
notes: State government operates at regional level in a federal system.
federal setup.
Maharashtra has a bicameral legislature: Vidhan Sabha (Legislative Assembly) and Vidhan Parishad (Legislative Council).
Vidhan Sabha has 288 members, elected from territorial constituencies, tenure of 5 years.
Vidhan Parishad has 78 members, indirectly elected, not fully dissolved; 1/3 retire every 2 years.
Governor is the nominal head of the state, appointed by the President, holds office during the President's pleasure.
Chief Minister is the real executive head, leader of the majority party in Vidhan Sabha, forms the Council of Ministers.
Council of Ministers includes portfolios distributed based on experience, skills, and representation of social groups.
Speaker of Vidhan Sabha presides over proceedings, elected by members, responsible for discipline and order.
Chief Minister coordinates ministries, ensures cooperation, and is collectively responsible to the Vidhan Sabha.
Governor can summon sessions, assent to bills, and issue ordinances when legislature is not in session.
State legislature makes laws on state subjects, approves budget, and oversees executive.
Judiciary protects individual rights, federal structure, and Constitution; has power of judicial review.
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) allows public-spirited individuals to approach courts for public causes.
Judicial activism refers to courts taking proactive role in safeguarding rights and ensuring justice.
First Information Report (FIR) is the first step in criminal procedure, filed with police for serious crimes.

quiz.q: Who is the nominal head of the state government in Maharashtra?
quiz.explain: The Governor is the nominal head of the state, appointed by the President.

quiz.q: What is the tenure of the Vidhan Sabha in Maharashtra?
quiz.explain: The Vidhan Sabha has a tenure of 5 years, unless dissolved earlier.

quiz.q: Which house of the Maharashtra legislature is never fully dissolved?
quiz.explain: The Vidhan Parishad is a permanent body; one-third of its members retire every two years.

quiz.q: Who appoints the Governor of a state in India?
quiz.explain: The Governor is appointed by the President of India.

quiz.q: Who is the real executive head of the state government?
quiz.explain: The Chief Minister is the real executive head and leads the Council of Ministers.

quiz.q: What is the minimum age to contest elections to the Vidhan Sabha?
quiz.explain: A citizen must be at least 25 years old to contest elections to the Vidhan Sabha.

quiz.q: Which session of the Maharashtra legislature is held in Nagpur?
quiz.explain: The winter session of the Maharashtra legislature is conducted in Nagpur.

quiz.q: What is the role of the Speaker in the Vidhan Sabha?
quiz.explain: The Speaker presides over the proceedings of the Vidhan Sabha and maintains order.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a provision to preserve judicial independence?
options: Security of tenure and fixed service conditions
Judges depend on legislature for salary
quiz.explain: Judicial independence is preserved by security of tenure and fixed service conditions.

quiz.q: What does Public Interest Litigation (PIL) allow?
options: Any public-spirited individual to file a case for public cause
Only the government to file cases
quiz.explain: PIL allows any public-spirited individual to approach the court for a cause affecting the public interest.

subject: History & Civics
notes: Bureaucracy is the administrative system of civil servants that implements government policies.
It is a permanent mechanism; civil servants remain in service despite changes in elected government.
Bureaucracy carries out two main functions: defense/security and public welfare/services.
Civil services in India are divided into All-India, Central (Union), and State services.
All-India Services include IAS, IPS, and IFS, recruited by UPSC and serving both Centre and States.
Union Civil Services include IRS, IFS, etc., serving under the Central Government.
State Civil Services include roles like Deputy Collector, Tehsildar, recruited by State PSC.
Civil servants are expected to be politically neutral and not align with any political party.
Anonymity means civil servants are not publicly credited or blamed; ministers take responsibility.
Merit-based recruitment is ensured by UPSC and State PSCs through competitive exams.
Reservation policy in civil services ensures representation of SC, ST, OBC, women, and disabled persons.
Civil servants provide expert advice to ministers, who are political heads but may lack technical knowledge.
Bureaucracy ensures stability in administration by maintaining continuity in governance.
It plays a key role in social transformation by implementing laws on welfare, education, and equality.
Effective minister-civil servant dialogue based on trust improves departmental functioning.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of bureaucracy in the context of government?
quiz.explain: Bureaucracy refers to the administrative system run by civil servants who implement government policies.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of bureaucracy?
quiz.explain: Making laws is the function of the legislature (Parliament), not bureaucracy.

quiz.q: Which service is responsible for maintaining law and order in a district?
quiz.explain: IPS officers are responsible for law and order and policing in states and districts.

quiz.q: What does 'permanent mechanism' mean in relation to bureaucracy?
options: Civil servants change with every election
Bureaucracy remains unchanged despite changes in government
quiz.explain: Bureaucracy is permanent; civil servants continue in service even when ministers change after elections.

quiz.q: Who is responsible for the success or failure of a government department?
quiz.explain: The minister, as political head, is accountable for departmental performance; civil servants remain anonymous.

quiz.q: Which body recruits candidates for All-India Services like IAS and IPS?
quiz.explain: UPSC conducts exams for All-India Services and Central Services.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of reservation in civil services?
options: To ensure representation of weaker sections
To promote only meritorious candidates regardless of background
quiz.explain: Reservation ensures that SC, ST, OBC, women, and disabled persons get fair access to civil services.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a State Civil Service?
quiz.explain: Deputy District Collector is a State Civil Service post under state government.

quiz.q: What does political neutrality of civil servants mean?
options: They must support the ruling party
They must not take political stands and serve any government impartially
They must join a political party after retirement
quiz.explain: Civil servants must serve the government in power with equal commitment, regardless of personal political views.

quiz.q: How does bureaucracy contribute to social transformation?
options: By implementing government policies on welfare and equality
quiz.explain: Bureaucracy implements laws related to women’s empowerment, education, reservation, etc., bringing social change.

subject: History & Civics
notes: Renaissance (13th-16th century) marked the revival of Greek and Roman ideas in Europe.
It brought changes in art, literature, science, and philosophy, promoting humanism.
Johannes Gutenberg invented the printing press around 1450 AD, spreading knowledge widely.
Leonardo da Vinci was a master of art, science, and engineering; famous for 'Monalisa' and 'The Last Supper'.
The Religious Reform movement challenged corrupt practices of the Roman Catholic Church.
Geographical discoveries were driven by the need to find new sea routes to Asia after Ottoman control of Constantinople.
In 1453, Ottoman Turks conquered Constantinople, blocking the land route to Asia.
Bartolomeu Dias reached the Cape of Good Hope in 1487 AD.
Christopher Columbus reached America in 1492 AD while seeking a western route to India.
Vasco da Gama reached Calicut, India in 1498 AD via the sea route around Africa.
The Industrial Revolution began in England in the 18th century with machine-based production.
It led to the rise of factories, steam power, railways, and the factory system.
Capitalism grew with new trade routes, leading to private investment and profit-driven economy.
Colonialism is when a powerful country controls another country and exploits its resources.
Imperialism is the policy of extending a country's power through colonization or military force.
British East India Company was established in 1600 AD to trade with India.
The Battle of Plassey (1757) gave the British control over Bengal after defeating Siraj-ud-Daulah.
The Battle of Buxar (1764) granted the British the right to collect revenue from Bengal.
The Anglo-Mysore Wars ended with British victory over Tipu Sultan in 1799.
The Anglo-Sikh Wars resulted in British annexation of Punjab by 1849.
The American War of Independence (1775-1783) led to the formation of the United States.
The French Revolution (1789) promoted liberty, equality, and fraternity, ending monarchy in France.
European rivalries in India led to the Carnatic Wars between the British and French.
The British eventually won dominance in India after defeating French and Indian powers.

quiz.q: In which year did the Ottoman Turks conquer Constantinople?
quiz.explain: Constantinople was conquered by the Ottoman Turks in 1453, which blocked the land route to Asia.

quiz.q: Who invented the printing press around 1450 AD?
quiz.explain: Johannes Gutenberg from Germany invented the printing press around 1450 AD, which helped spread knowledge.

quiz.q: Which Portuguese sailor reached the Indian coast at Calicut in 1498?
quiz.explain: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 by sailing around the Cape of Good Hope, establishing the sea route to India.

quiz.q: What was the main reason for European countries to seek new sea routes to Asia?
options: To find new lands for settlement
quiz.explain: After the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople in 1453, they blocked the land route to Asia, prompting Europeans to find sea routes.

quiz.q: Which event is known as the 'Age of Revolutions'?
quiz.explain: The 18th and 19th centuries saw major political changes like the American and French Revolutions, hence called the Age of Revolutions.

quiz.q: Which values were promoted by the French Revolution?
quiz.explain: The French Revolution of 1789 stood for the ideals of Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity.

quiz.q: In which year was the British East India Company established?
quiz.explain: The British East India Company was established in 1600 AD to carry out trade with India.

quiz.q: Which battle gave the British the right to collect revenue from Bengal?
quiz.explain: After the Battle of Buxar in 1764, the British East India Company gained the right to collect revenue from Bengal via the Treaty of Allahabad.

quiz.q: What does colonialism mean?
options: One country exploiting another by making it a colony
quiz.explain: Colonialism means a powerful country controls another country and exploits its resources and people.

quiz.q: Which revolution began in England with the use of machines and steam power?
quiz.explain: The Industrial Revolution began in England in the 18th century, marked by machine-based production and steam power.

subject: History & Civics
notes: British East India Company came to India for trade but later established political control.
The Subsidiary Alliance (1798) by Lord Wellesley required Indian rulers to accept British troops in their state and not ally with any other power.
The Treaty of Vasai (1802) was signed by Bajirao II with the British, leading to loss of Maratha independence.
Dual Government in Bengal (1765) meant the Company collected revenue while the Nawab maintained law and order.
Lord Cornwallis introduced bureaucratic reforms and restricted private trade of Company officers.
Civil Services were introduced to bring efficiency; recruitment was through competitive examinations.
The Military and Police were used to protect British interests and suppress revolts.
A new Judicial system was set up based on English model, with Civil and Criminal Courts in districts and High Courts for appeals.
Equality before law was introduced, ending caste-based differences in legal judgments.
Land revenue systems varied by region; tax was fixed in cash based on land measurement, leading to farmer exploitation.
Farmers often sold crops at low prices, mortgaged land, or became bankrupt due to revenue demands.
British economic policies ruined traditional industries by imposing heavy taxes on Indian goods and promoting British machine-made imports.
Commercialisation of agriculture shifted focus from food grains to cash crops like cotton, indigo, tea for export to England.
Transport and communication developed: railways (1853), telegraph, postal system improved administration and trade.
Social reforms included abolition of Sati (1829), Widow Remarriage Act (1856), and spread of Western education after 1835.
Universities were established in Kolkata, Mumbai, and Chennai in 1857.
British studied Indian society to govern better, leading to growth of societies like Asiatic Society of Bengal.
Western-educated Indians led social reform movements in the 19th century.
Economic exploitation caused famines; British did little to relieve suffering during famines from 1860–1900.
New industries like textiles (Mumbai, 1854), jute (Bengal, 1855), and steel (Tata, Jamshedpur, 1907) began under Indian initiative despite limited British support.

quiz.q: Who introduced the Subsidiary Alliance system in India?
quiz.explain: Lord Wellesley introduced the Subsidiary Alliance in 1798 to bring Indian states under British control.

quiz.q: Which Maratha ruler signed the Subsidiary Alliance with the British in 1802?
quiz.explain: Bajirao II signed the Subsidiary Alliance with the British in 1802, known as the Treaty of Vasai.

quiz.q: What was the main feature of the Dual Government system in Bengal introduced by Robert Clive in 1765?
options: Company collected revenue, Nawab maintained law and order
Nawab collected revenue, Company maintained army
Company controlled army, Nawab collected taxes
Both revenue and law under Company
quiz.explain: Under Dual Government, the East India Company collected revenue while the Nawab of Bengal was responsible for civil administration and law and order.

quiz.q: Which act made the Governor of Bengal the Governor General of India?
quiz.explain: The Regulating Act of 1773 made the Governor of Bengal the Governor General of India, with Warren Hastings as the first holder.

quiz.q: What was the main source of state income during the Pre-British period in India?
quiz.explain: During the Pre-British period, land revenue was the main source of state income, based on the type of cultivated crop.

quiz.q: Under the new land revenue system, if a farmer failed to pay tax in time, what could happen?
quiz.explain: If a farmer failed to pay land revenue in time, his land could be confiscated by the British authorities.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a result of the commercialisation of agriculture in British India?
options: Shift to cash crops for export
quiz.explain: Commercialisation of agriculture meant farmers were encouraged to grow cash crops like cotton, indigo, and tea for export to England instead of food grains.

quiz.q: Which act prohibited the practice of Sati in India?
quiz.explain: Lord William Bentinck passed the Sati Prohibition Act in 1829, banning the practice of Sati.

quiz.q: In which year was the first railway line opened in India, running from Mumbai to Thane?
quiz.explain: The first railway in India ran from Mumbai to Thane in 1853.

quiz.q: Who established the Tata Iron and Steel Company at Jamshedpur?
quiz.explain: Jamsetji Tata founded the Tata Iron and Steel Company in Jamshedpur in 1907.

subject: History & Civics
notes: Prarthana Samaj was founded by Dadoba Pandurang Tarkhadkar in 1848 to promote social reform and eradicate superstitions.
It opposed idol worship, rituals, and caste discrimination, and encouraged education and social welfare.
Brahmo Samaj, started by Raja Rammohan Roy in 1828, focused on monotheism, opposed caste, and promoted women's education.
Satyashodhak Samaj, founded by Jyotirao Phule in 1873, worked for equality, widow remarriage, and education of the depressed classes.
Arya Samaj, established by Swami Dayanand Saraswati in 1875, promoted return to Vedic teachings and opposed casteism.
Ramkrishna Mission, founded by Swami Vivekananda in 1897, emphasized service to humanity and education.
Maharshi Vitthal Ramji Shinde organized the Depressed Classes Mission to uplift untouchables.
Mahatma Savitribai Phule established the first school for girls in Pune and fought for women's education.
Maharshi Karve founded the first women's university, Sharda Sadan, in 1925.
The movement of religious reform in India was driven by leaders who used education, literature, and public speeches to spread ideas.

quiz.q: Which society was founded by Dadoba Pandurang Tarkhadkar in 1848?
quiz.explain: Dadoba Tarkhadkar established Prarthana Samaj in 1848.

quiz.q: What was the main slogan of Arya Samaj?
quiz.explain: Arya Samaj’s slogan was ‘Go Back to the Vedas’.

quiz.q: Which reformer founded the Depressed Classes Mission?
quiz.explain: Maharshi Vitthal Ramji Shinde organized the Depressed Classes Mission.

quiz.q: Ramkrishna Mission was established in which year?
quiz.explain: Ramkrishna Mission was founded by Swami Vivekananda in 1897.

quiz.q: Which society opposed child marriage and dowry?
quiz.explain: Satyashodhak Samaj fought against child marriage and dowry.

quiz.q: Who wrote the book ‘Satyarth Prakash’?
quiz.explain: Swami Dayanand Saraswati wrote ‘Satyarth Prakash’.

quiz.q: Which movement was led by the Singh Sabha?
quiz.explain: Singh Sabha worked for reforms in Sikh religion.

quiz.q: The first women's university in India was established by whom?
quiz.explain: Maharshi Karve founded Sharda Sadan, the first women's university.

quiz.q: Which reformer is known for the slogan ‘Arise, Awake and Stop Not Till Goal is Achieved’?
quiz.explain: Swami Vivekananda used this slogan.

quiz.q: The Ramkrishna Mission’s first school for girls was established in which city?
quiz.explain: Mahatma Phule started the first girls’ school in Pune.

subject: History & Civics
notes: - Western education introduced new ideas of justice, liberty, equality and democracy to India.
- British administration centralized power, built roads and railways, and introduced English as a common language.
- Economic exploitation: cash crops, high land taxes, famines, decline of traditional industries and rise in unemployment.
- Newspapers and periodicals (e.g., Darpan, Kesari, Amrit Bazar Patrika) spread nationalist ideas and criticised the British.
- Indian National Congress (INC) was formed in 1885 to give a platform for Indians to express demands and seek constitutional reforms.
- INC had two phases: Moderate (1885‑1905) and Extremist (1905‑1920). Moderates used peaceful constitutional methods; Extremists used more aggressive tactics like boycotts and public agitation.
- Key moderate leaders: Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee, Ferozshah Mehta, Lala Lajpat Rai.
- Key extremist leaders: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lokmanya Tilak.
- Partition of Bengal (1905) was a British ‘divide and rule’ strategy that intensified nationalist sentiment and led to the Swadeshi movement.
- The Home Rule movement (1905‑1909) demanded self‑government for India; it was led by Annie Besant and Lokmanya Tilak.
- The Lucknow Pact (1916) was an agreement between INC and the Muslim League to cooperate for Muslim rights and Indian self‑rule.
- The Montagu‑Chelmsford Reforms (1919) introduced limited self‑government but disappointed many Indians.
- The Servants of India Society (founded 1905 by Gopal Krishna Gokhale) aimed to promote social harmony and national service.
- The anti‑partition movement in Bengal was called the ‘Geeta Rahasya’ movement, encouraging continuous public agitation.
- The Swadeshi movement promoted the boycott of foreign goods and the use of Indian products.
- The Indian National Congress split in 1907 into the Moderate and Extremist groups, leading to different strategies for independence.

quiz.q: Which of the following was NOT a reason for the British to centralize administration in India?
quiz.explain: Centralization helped Britain control India, not promote self‑government.

quiz.q: Who founded the Servants of India Society in 1905?
quiz.explain: Gopal Krishna Gokhale established the society.

quiz.q: The partition of Bengal in 1905 was mainly intended to:
options: Create a Hindu majority in Bengal
quiz.explain: It was a divide‑and‑rule strategy.

quiz.q: Which movement encouraged the boycott of foreign goods?
quiz.explain: Swadeshi promoted Indian products.

quiz.q: The Lucknow Pact was signed in which year?
quiz.explain: It was signed in 1916.

quiz.q: Who was a moderate leader of the Indian National Congress?
quiz.explain: Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a moderate.

quiz.q: Which of the following was a newspaper used by extremists to criticize the British?
quiz.explain: Darpan was used by extremists.

quiz.q: The Montagu‑Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 introduced:
quiz.explain: They introduced limited self‑government.

quiz.q: The anti‑partition movement in Bengal was also known as:
quiz.explain: It was called the Geeta Rahasya movement.

quiz.q: Which leader was imprisoned in Mandalay jail for 6 years?
quiz.explain: Tilak was imprisoned in Mandalay jail.

subject: History & Civics
notes: - The Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑1922) was a mass campaign led by Mahatma Gandhi to protest British rule in India.
- It was the first large‑scale, nationwide movement where Indians refused to buy British goods, attend British schools, or use British courts.
- The movement was based on the principle of Satyagraha – non‑violent resistance and truth.
- Key events: Champaran Satyagraha (1917), Kheda Satyagraha (1918), Mulshi Satyagraha (1920), and the nationwide boycott of government offices and schools.
- Gandhi’s slogan: “Quit India” was later adopted in 1942, but during 1920‑22 the focus was on non‑cooperation and civil disobedience.
- The movement was halted in February 1922 after the Chauri Chaura incident, where a mob set fire to a police station, killing 22 officers.
- The movement helped spread Swadeshi (home‑made goods), khadi, and Hindu‑Muslim unity.
- The Swaraj Party was formed in 1922 by Congress leaders who wanted to contest elections and obstruct British administration from within.
- The movement ended with Gandhi’s release from jail in 1924 and the start of the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930.
- Key terms: Satyagraha, Swadeshi, Khadi, Mulshi, Chauri Chaura, Non‑Cooperation Movement, Swaraj Party, Simon Commission, Nehru Report, Khilafat Movement.

quiz.q: What was the main goal of the Non‑Cooperation Movement?
options: To demand a separate state for Muslims
To boycott British goods and institutions
To create a new political party
quiz.explain: The movement aimed to boycott British goods, schools, courts and offices.

quiz.q: Which event led to the suspension of the movement in 1922?
quiz.explain: The Chauri Chaura fire caused 22 police deaths, prompting Gandhi to halt the movement.

quiz.q: Who was the leader of the Swaraj Party formed in 1922?
quiz.explain: Motilal Nehru was a key founder of the Swaraj Party.

quiz.q: What was the slogan used by the Non‑Cooperation Movement?
quiz.explain: The slogan “Quit India” was later used; during 1920‑22 the slogan was “Non‑cooperation”.

quiz.q: Which movement was launched by Gandhi in Champaran?
quiz.explain: Champaran Satyagraha was the first mass protest led by Gandhi in 1917.

quiz.q: The Khilafat Movement was started to support which leader?
quiz.explain: It aimed to support the Caliph (Khalifa) of Turkey.

quiz.q: Which act was known as the ‘Black Act’?
quiz.explain: The Rowlatt Act was called the ‘Black Act’ by Indians.

quiz.q: What was the main consequence of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre?
options: Increased support for the Rowlatt Act
quiz.explain: The massacre sparked the Non‑Cooperation Movement.

quiz.q: Which of the following was NOT a feature of the Non‑Cooperation Movement?
quiz.explain: The movement opposed participation in British elections.

quiz.q: Who was the British officer that ordered the firing at Jallianwala Bagh?
quiz.explain: General Dyer ordered the firing.

subject: History & Civics
notes: Civil Disobedience Movement was a non‑violent protest against British laws, especially the Salt Act of 1930.
Mahatma Gandhi launched the movement on 5 April 1930 by breaking the salt law at Dandi, Gujarat.
The act of breaking the salt law was called the Salt Satyagraha or Salt March.
Gandhi’s march covered about 385 km from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, with 78 followers.
The movement spread to all parts of India – urban, rural, tribal and women participated in large numbers.
Key leaders included Kasturba Gandhi, Sarojini Naidu, Khan Abdul Gafar Khan (Frontier Gandhi) and Babu Genu.
The British responded with arrests, lathi charges, martial law and even death in some cases (e.g., Babu Genu).
The movement inspired other acts of non‑violent resistance such as the Dharasana Satyagraha and the Solapur Satyagraha.
The Indian National Congress withdrew from the Round Table Conferences (1930‑32) to focus on the movement.
The movement ended in 1934 when Gandhi decided to restart it after being released from prison.
The movement was based on complete non‑violence, truth (satya) and self‑discipline (satyagraha).
Women’s participation was significant; Kasturba Gandhi, Kamladevi Chattopadhyay, and others led protests.
The movement led to the Gandhi‑Irwin Pact (1932) and the Poona Pact, addressing separate electorates for Dalits.
The movement demonstrated the power of mass civil disobedience and the willingness of Indians to suffer for freedom.
Gandhi’s strategy combined moral force, mass participation, and symbolic acts to challenge British authority.
The movement highlighted the importance of unity across caste, class, and gender lines.
The movement’s success depended on the willingness of ordinary people to follow Gandhi’s example.
The movement showed that non‑violent protest could force political negotiations with the British.
The movement was a key phase in India’s struggle for independence, preceding the Quit India Movement of 1942.
The movement’s legacy continues to inspire civil rights movements worldwide.
Key terms: Satyagraha, Salt March, Dharasana Satyagraha, Solapur Satyagraha, Round Table Conference, Gandhi‑Irwin Pact, Poona Pact.

quiz.q: What was the main objective of the Salt Satyagraha launched by Gandhi in 1930?
options: To protest the Indian National Congress policies
To break the British salt tax and monopoly
To demand separate electorates for Dalits
To establish a new salt factory in India
quiz.explain: Gandhi broke the salt law to protest the salt tax and monopoly imposed by the British.

quiz.q: Which leader was known as 'Frontier Gandhi' and led the Peshawar Satyagraha?
quiz.explain: Khan Abdul Gafar Khan was called 'Frontier Gandhi' and organized the Peshawar Satyagraha.

quiz.q: What was the response of the British government to the Salt Satyagraha?
options: They immediately lifted the salt tax
They arrested Gandhi and used lathi charges
quiz.explain: The British arrested Gandhi and used lathi charges against protesters.

quiz.q: Which pact was signed between Gandhi and the Viceroy in 1932?
quiz.explain: The Gandhi‑Irwin Pact was signed in 1932 between Gandhi and the Viceroy.

quiz.q: The Poona Pact addressed which issue?
quiz.explain: The Poona Pact ended separate electorates for Dalits and provided reserved seats.

quiz.q: What was the main strategy of the Civil Disobedience Movement?
quiz.explain: The movement used non‑violent protest (satyagraha) to challenge British laws.

quiz.q: Which event marked the beginning of the Salt Satyagraha?
quiz.explain: The Dandi march on 5 April 1930 marked the start of the Salt Satyagraha.

quiz.q: Why did the Indian National Congress withdraw from the Round Table Conferences?
options: They wanted to focus on the Civil Disobedience Movement
They were satisfied with the British proposals
They were forced to leave by the British
quiz.explain: The Congress withdrew to concentrate on the Civil Disobedience Movement.

quiz.q: Who was Babu Genu?
options: A mill worker who was martyred
quiz.explain: Babu Genu was a mill worker who was crushed by a truck while protesting.

quiz.q: Which of the following was NOT a feature of the Civil Disobedience Movement?
quiz.explain: The movement was based on non‑violence; it did not use violence.

subject: History & Civics
chapter: Last Phase of Struggle for Independence
notes: - The Quit India Movement began on 8 August 1942 and was a nationwide, non‑violent protest demanding immediate independence.
- It was launched by the Indian National Congress under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru.
- The movement called for the British to leave India, release political prisoners, end prohibition of liquor, and grant full self‑rule.
- The British responded by arresting leaders, closing offices, and using force against protesters.
- Despite the crackdown, millions participated; many were imprisoned and some died in the struggle.
- Parallel governments were set up in some districts, providing local administration and inspiring people.
- The Indian National Army (INA), led by Subhash Chandra Bose, fought against the British with Japanese support.
- The INA captured some territories and established the Azad Hind Government in Singapore in 1943.
- The Indian Navy and Air Force also staged revolts, notably the 1946 ‘Talwar’ incident where sailors raised the tricolor.
- The Quit India Movement is also called the ‘August Kranti’ (August Revolution).

quiz.q: What was the main demand of the Quit India Resolution passed by the Congress in 1942?
options: Immediate independence and release of political prisoners
Joining the war on the side of Britain
quiz.explain: The resolution demanded immediate independence and the release of political prisoners.

quiz.q: Who was the leader of the Indian National Army that fought against the British?
quiz.explain: Subhash Chandra Bose led the INA.

quiz.q: Which event is also known as the ‘August Kranti’?
quiz.explain: The Quit India Movement is called the August Kranti.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the Parallel Government set up during the Quit India Movement?
options: To provide local governance and inspire people
quiz.explain: The Parallel Government offered local administration and inspired the masses.

quiz.q: Which of the following was NOT a part of the Quit India Movement’s demands?
options: Joining the war on the side of Britain
quiz.explain: The movement did not ask the British to join the war.

quiz.q: Which Indian leader was arrested during the Quit India Movement and later released in 1945?
quiz.explain: Mahatma Gandhi was arrested and released in 1945.

quiz.q: The ‘Talwar’ incident in 1946 involved which branch of the armed forces?
quiz.explain: The incident involved the Indian Navy.

quiz.q: Which organization was founded by Subhash Chandra Bose after resigning from the Congress?
quiz.explain: Bose founded the Forward Bloc.

quiz.q: The Indian National Army was also known by which name?
quiz.explain: The INA was called Azad Hind Sena.

quiz.q: Which event marked the beginning of the Quit India Movement?
quiz.explain: The movement began after the resolution at Wardha.

subject: History & Civics
notes: - Armed revolutionary movement: a form of struggle where Indians used weapons and violent acts to fight British rule.
- Key organisations: Abhinav Bharat, Anushilan Samiti, India House, Gadar (Kakori) movement, Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA).
- Abhinav Bharat (1900): secret society founded by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, aimed to create armed revolution.
- Anushilan Samiti (Bengal): underground group that trained members in bomb-making and sabotage.
- India House (London, 1908): hub for Indian students abroad, funded revolutionary activities in India.
- Gadar movement (1915): Indian revolutionaries in North America formed a bank to fund armed rebellion in India.
- HSRA (1920s): youth-led group that carried out bomb attacks in the Central Legislative Assembly and planned the Chittagong Armoury Raid.
- Chittagong Armoury Raid (1930): led by Surya Sen, aimed to seize arms from two police armories in Chittagong, Bengal.
- Kakori conspiracy (1925): train robbery near Lucknow to raise funds for revolution.
- Important figures: Vinayak Savarkar, Rash Behari Bose, Khudiram Bose, Prafulla Chaki, Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev, Chandrashekhar Azad, Surya Sen, Pritilata Waddedar.
- Methods: bomb attacks, assassinations, train robbery, sabotage, underground printing of pamphlets.
- Goals: overthrow British rule, end social injustices, establish a free India.
- Impact: inspired many, led to harsher British repression, but kept revolutionary spirit alive.
- Key dates: 1900 (Abhinav Bharat), 1908 (India House), 1915 (Gadar), 1925 (Kakori), 1930 (Chittagong raid).
- Remember: Revolutionaries often faced imprisonment, torture, and execution; many became martyrs.
- The movement was not a single plan but a series of coordinated attacks across India and abroad.
- The British response included stricter laws, increased police surveillance, and mass arrests.
- Legacy: These revolutionary acts are remembered as part of India's struggle for independence.

शेतकरी चळवळ ब्रिटिशांच्या आर्थिक धोरणामुळे शेतकऱ्यांना झालेल्या अन्यायावर आधारित होती.
साने गुरुजी, रामचंद्र, अंमळनेर गिरणी कामगार युनियनचे अध्यक्ष हे शेतकरी व कामगार चळवळीतील प्रमुख नेते होते.
किसान सभा, कामगार संघटना, महिला समाज अशा विविध संघटनांनी शेतकरी, कामगार व स्त्रियांच्या हितासाठी कार्य केले.
महात्मा फुले, नारायण गुरू यांनी दलितांना अस्पृश्यतेपासून मुक्त करण्यासाठी शिक्षण व स्वाभिमानाची प्रेरणा दिली.

notes: स्वातंत्र्यप्राप्ती म्हणजे 15 ऑगस्ट 1947 रोजी भारताला ब्रिटनकडून स्वातंत्र्य मिळाले.
भारताचे स्वातंत्र्य 1947 मध्ये झाले, परंतु 1948 मध्ये भारताची स्वतंत्रता पूर्ण झाली.
स्वातंत्र्याच्या प्रक्रियेत तीन महत्त्वाच्या योजना होत्या – त्रिमंत्री योजना, वेव्हेल योजना आणि हंगामी सरकार योजना.
त्रिमंत्री योजना 1946 मध्ये ब्रिटनने भारताला तीन मंत्र्यांना (बंगाल, पंतप्रधान, परराष्ट्र) अधिकार दिले.
वेव्हेल योजना 1945 मध्ये व्हाईसरॉय लॉर्ड वेव्हेल यांनी तयार केली, ज्यात मुस्लीम लीगला प्रतिनिधित्व दिले गेले.
हंगामी सरकार योजना 1947 मध्ये ब्रिटनने भारतात तात्पुरती सरकार स्थापन केली, ज्याचे प्रमुख न्ही. जावाहरलाल नेहरू होते.
मुस्लीम लीगने पाकिस्तानची मागणी केली, ज्यामुळे भारताची फाळणी झाली.
फाळणीमुळे 15 ऑगस्ट 1947 रोजी भारत आणि पाकिस्तान हे दोन स्वतंत्र राष्ट्र बनले.

subject: History & Civics
notes: भारताला १९४७ मध्ये स्वातंत्र्य मिळाल्यानंतर भाषावार प्रांतरचना मागणी सुरू झाली.
१९४८ मध्ये काँग्रेसने भाषावार प्रांतरचना समिती (जे.व्ही.पी. समिती) गठित केली.
जे.व्ही.पी. समितीने १९४९ मध्ये अहवाल दाखल केला, पण त्याने भाषावार प्रांतरचना नाकारली.
१९५३ मध्ये नागपूर करार केला, जिथे मराठी भाषिक प्रदेशाची मागणी केली गेली.
१९५५ मध्ये राज्य पुनर्रचना आयोग (फजल अली आयोग)ने अहवाल दाखल केला, जिथे संयुक्त महाराष्ट्राची शिफारस केली.
१९५६ मध्ये संयुक्त महाराष्ट्र समितीची स्थापना केली, जिला मराठी भाषिक राज्याची मागणी करण्यासाठी.
१ नोव्हेंबर १९५६ रोजी दुविभाषिक मुंबई राज्य निर्माण केला गेला.
१ मे १९६० रोजी महाराष्ट्र राज्याची निर्मिती झाली, जिथे गुजरात पृथक झाला.
यशवंतराव चव्हाण महाराष्ट्राचे पहिले मुख्यमंत्री झाले.
संयुक्त महाराष्ट्र आंदोलनात सेनापती बापट, नाना पाटील, लालजी पेंडसे, अहिल्याबाई रांगणेकर यांचे योगदान मोठा होता.
आंदोलनात कामगार मैदानावर मोठी सभा झाली, जिथे शंकरराव देवने मुंबई वेगळी करण्याचा विरोध केला.
आंदोलनात १०६ हुतात्मा झाले, ज्यांची स्मरक म्हणून फ्लोरा फाऊंटनमध्ये हुतात्मा स्मारक स्थापित केला.
वृत्तपत्रे व शाहिरे (जसे केसरी, सकाळ, अण्णाभाऊ साठे)ने जनजागृतीमध्ये महत्त्वपूर्ण भूमिका निभाली.
विधानसभा व मुंबई महानगरपालिकेच्या निवडणुका समितीने संयुक्त महाराष्ट्र समितीला समर्थन दिला.
१९६० एप्रिल मध्ये संसदेने मुंबई पुनर्रचना कायदा मंजूर केला, ज्यामुळे १ मे १९६० रोजी महाराष्ट्र राज्याची निर्मिती झाली.

quiz.explain: भारताला स्वातंत्र्य मिळाल्यानंतर प्रांतरचना मागणी भाषावार आधारावर सुरू झाली.

quiz.explain: जे.व्ही.पी. समिती काँग्रेसने २९ डिसेंबर १९४८ रोजी गठित केली.

quiz.explain: नागपूर करार १९५३ मध्ये केला गेला, जिथे मराठी भाषिक प्रदेशाची मागणी केली गेली.

quiz.q: राज्य पुनर्रचना आयोग (फजल अली आयोग)ने अहवाल कधी दाखल केला?
quiz.explain: राज्य पुनर्रचना आयोगने १० ऑक्टोबर १९५५ रोजी अहवाल सादर केला.

quiz.q: संयुक्त महाराष्ट्र समितीची स्थापना कधी केली?
quiz.explain: संयुक्त महाराष्ट्र समितीची स्थापना १ नोव्हेंबर १९५६ रोजी केली.

quiz.q: महाराष्ट्र राज्याची निर्मिती कधी झाली?
quiz.explain: महाराष्ट्र राज्याची निर्मिती १ मे १९६० रोजी झाली.

quiz.q: महाराष्ट्राचे पहिले मुख्यमंत्री कोणते झाले?
quiz.explain: यशवंतराव चव्हाण महाराष्ट्राचे पहिले मुख्यमंत्री झाले.

quiz.q: संयुक्त महाराष्ट्र आंदोलनात कोणती महिलांची सहभागी उल्लेखनीय होती?
quiz.explain: सुमतीबाई गोरे, इस्मत चुगताई, दुर्‍गा भागवत व इतर महिलांनी संयुक्त महाराष्ट्र आंदोलनात सहभागी होऊन योगदान दिला.
